Systematic construction of stabilizer codes via gauging abelian boundary symmetries
Bram Vancraeynest-De Cuiper, José Garre-Rubio

Abstract
We propose a systematic framework to construct a (d+1)-dimensional stabilizer model from an initial generic d-dimensional abelian symmetry. Our approach builds upon the iterative gauging procedure , developed by one of the authors in [J. Garre-Rubio, Nature Commun. 15 , 7986 (2024)] , in which an initial symmetric state is repeatedly gauged to obtain an emergent model in one dimension higher that supports the initial symmetry at its boundary. This method not only enables the construction of emergent states and corresponding commuting stabilizer Hamiltonians of which they are ground states, but it also provides a way to construct gapped boundary conditions for these models that amount to spontaneously breaking part of the boundary symmetry. In a detailed introductory example, we showcase our paradigm by constructing three-dimensional Clifford-deformed surface codes from iteratively gauging a global 0-form symmetry that lives in two dimensions. We then provide a proof of our main result, hereby drawing upon a slight extension of the gauging procedure of Williamson. We additionally provide two more examples in d=2 in which different type-I fracton orders emerge from gauging initial linear subsystem and Sierpinski fractal symmetries. En passant, we provide explicit tensor network representations of all of the involved gauging maps and the emergent states.



Introduction

Different incarnations of
bulk-boundary correspondence
are ubiquitous in condensed matter physics. Generically, a bulk-boundary correspondence establishes a relation between the non-trivial physics in the bulk of a certain physical system and the physics constrained to its boundary. One example of such a relation is the conjecture that the bulk of certain
anomaly-free
topological orders is fully determined by their gapped boundary theory by means of an appropriate notion of the categorical
center

[
1
,
2
,
3
]
. A bulk-boundary correspondence has also proven to be the key for finding cohomological invariants that differentiate certain symmetry-protected topological phases (SPTs) protected by an invertible symmetry, whereby these invariants pertain to the transformation properties of the edge modes under the symmetry group. For the particular case of (1+1)d, this approach has led to a complete classification of gapped one-dimensional phases with group-like symmetry
[
4
,
5
]
. More recently, it has also been argued how the boundaries of particular fracton phases host
emergent
subsystem symmetries whose explicit realization can be traced back to the characteristics of the bulk excitation spectrum
[
6
]
. Contrary to the case of intrinsic topological orders, it was demonstrated that the
bulk reconstruction
of the fracton orders under scrutiny depends in a non-trivial way on the relative orientation of the boundary with respect to the bulk. In a certain sense all of the above examples of bulk-boundary correspondence can thus be brought together under the umbrella term of a
holographic principle
.

In another recent series of developments an opposite avenue has been pursued in which a given quantum field theory (QFT) with a (higher)
categorical symmetry
is regarded as an interval compactification of a topological field theory in one dimension higher, coined ‘SymTFT’, with a
topological
gapped boundary condition determining the symmetry of the QFT and a not necessarily gapped
physical
boundary condition that dictates the dynamics of the QFT
[
7
,
8
]
. In this picture the focus is very much on the understanding of certain features of the symmetric QFT, such as (dis)order parameters, gapped phases and anomalies, from the higher-dimensional SymTFT. Aspects of this paradigm have previously appeared under the name of ‘strange correlator’, which admits an explicit lattice realization in terms of tensor network representations of the higher-dimensional topological order
[
9
,
10
,
11
]
.

In this manuscript we realize an explicit bulk-boundary correspondence for generic abelian
boundary symmetries
in any dimension by making use of the
iterative gauging procedure
proposed by one of the authors in
[
12
]
for
one-dimensional abelian boundary symmetries
. That work builds on the observation that gauging an
initial
abelian (anomaly-free global 0-form) symmetry gives rise to
dual
on-site global symmetry generators labeled by the one-dimensional representations of the underlying symmetry group. Since this emergent symmetry is on-site, a tensor product of local unitaries, it is free of any ’t Hooft anomaly, and so it can be gauged, thereby recovering the initial
G
symmetry. The crux of the paradigm put forward in
[
12
]
is that these gauging procedures can be repeated indefinitely and that in this way a state emerges which naturally lives in one dimension higher than the initial symmetry. Such an
emergent state
was shown in
[
12
]
to be stabilized by certain local operators whose origin can be traced back to the Gauss constraints of the involved gauging procedures. In this picture, the initial symmetry which is being gauged can be thought of as a
boundary symmetry
for the emergent state. This idea is made very tangible by making use of the explicit
gauging map
for quantum states proposed in
[
13
]
and generalized later in
[
14
]
. One of the main advantages of using this approach is that a tensor network description of the gauging maps is readily available, which can in turn be used to write down an explicit tensor network representation of the emergent state, facilitating the analytical study of its properties and its numerical simulation.

In the current manuscript, Ref.
[
12
]
is extended to arbitrary dimensions and generic abelian symmetries. Specifically, we propose a slight generalization of the gauging procedure of
[
14
]
to arbitrary abelian groups, and demonstrate that the iterative gauging procedure of
[
12
]
in
any dimension
gives rise to emergent states with corresponding
local stabilizer
Hamiltonians. The abelian symmetries which are being gauged in the framework of
[
14
]
are completely specified by a
complete collection
of ‘checks’ which commute with all symmetry generators. As such, that framework includes the gauging of
fractal
and
subsystem
symmetries as specific cases. In our general framework we are also able to relate inequivalent choices of
gapped boundary stabilizers
to different spontaneous symmetry breaking patters of the boundary symmetry.

To showcase our framework we provide three detailed worked examples where the initial boundary symmetry is two-dimensional. Gauging a global on-site
0-form
symmetry in (2+1)d gives rise to emergent
1-form
– or
Wilson loop
– symmetries. In this case the iterative gauging framework gives rise to three-dimensional
Clifford-deformed surface codes

[
15
]
, which are up to a local basis change equivalent to the three-dimensional abelian quantum doubles
[
16
]
. Two-dimensional linear subsystem symmetries map to dual linear subsystem symmetries on the dual lattice. Applying the framework in this case gives rise to foliated anisotropic type-I fracton orders
[
17
]
. Finally, we leverage the full potential of our framework and the gauging procedure of
[
14
]
to gauge fractal boundary symmetry, specifically of Sierpinski type, and obtain the fracton model proposed by Caselnovo and Chamon in
[
18
]
for the study of quantum glassiness. For each of these examples we also provide a tensor network description of the involved gauging maps, and hence the emergent state, which is based on the tensor network description of the gauging map for global on-site 0-form symmetries of
[
13
]
.

Our manuscript is organized as follows. In
we provide an introductory example to explicitly demonstrate the iterative gauging procedure applied to an initial two-dimensional global on-site symmetry. All the details of our framework including the study of symmetry-breaking boundary conditions and the tensor network representation of the emergent Clifford-deformed CSS codes are discussed in detail. This section also serves as an introduction to many of the conventions and notations used throughout this manuscript. We then proceed by putting these observations on systematic footing in
. First, we slightly generalize the gauging procedure of
[
14
]
to generic abelian groups and then prove that the iterative gauging procedure in any dimension gives rise to emergent states with a corresponding commuting stabilizer Hamiltonian of which it is a ground state. We then provide a way to add boundary stabilizers to the emergent Hamiltonian which commute with all terms in the bulk and among each other, thereby preserving the gap. We argue that different gapped boundary stabilizers correspond to certain symmetry breaking patterns of the boundary symmetry. We then conclude with two more examples in
and
that pertain to the derivation of different type-I fracton models from the iterative gauging of linear subsystem boundary symmetry and Sierpinski fractal symmetry respectively.

Iterative gauging

Figure 1:
Schematic overview of the iterative gauging procedure. Given a d-dimensional symmetric state, iterative gauging of its symmetry and the emerging dual symmetries give rise to a (d+1)-dimensional stabilizer model with the initial state as boundary.

1
Introductory example:

Clifford-deformed surface codes from abelian higher-form symmetries

In this section we review the gauging procedure of abelian on-site global 0-form symmetries proposed in
[
13
]
for two-dimensional symmetric states. We argue that the gauged state is in the even sector of a dual global 1-form
\widehat{G}
symmetry acting non-trivially solely on the introduced gauge degrees of freedom. We use an explicit gauging procedure for this 1-form symmetry, following refs.
[
19
,
14
]
, that yields in turn again the original
G
symmetry. For both gauging maps we construct a tensor network representation of bond dimension
|G|
. We show that the concatenation of these 2D gauging maps as in
[
12
]
produces 3D Clifford-deformed surface codes
[
15
]
, which are unitarily equivalent to abelian
G
quantum doubles
[
16
]
.

\bullet

Let us consider the two-dimensional torus endowed with a lattice
\Lambda
, whose sets of vertices, oriented edges and plaquettes will be denoted by
\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)
,
\mathsf{E}(\Lambda)
and
\mathsf{P}(\Lambda)
respectively. The starting point of the gauging procedure laid out in
[
13
]
is then a two-dimensional state
\ket{\psi}
living in a tensor product Hilbert space of the so-called
matter
degrees of freedom supported on the vertices of
\Lambda
,
\ket{\psi}\in\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)}\mathcal{H}^{\mathsf{v}}
. The local Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}^{\mathsf{v}}
forms a unitary representation of
G
, which is assumed to be abelian throughout the manuscript, and whose matrix representation is written as
\{u_{g}|g\in G\}
. We adapt the notation
\overline{g}
to denote the inverse group element of
g\in G
and
1
to denote the identity element. The state
\ket{\psi}
is then required to transform trivially under the tensor product representation
\{\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)}u_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}|g\in G\}
1
1

1

Indeed, if
\ket{\psi}
transforms non-trivially under
G
, the gauging map defined below annihilates
\ket{\psi}
. However, a different gauging map can be defined for each symmetry sector.
, i.e.:

\bigg(\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)}u_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}\bigg)\ket{\psi}=\ket{\psi},\quad\forall g\in G.

(1.1)

Notice that the symmetry operators considered here act on all matter degrees of freedom
\mathcal{H}^{\mathsf{v}}
,
\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)
, simultaneously. Such a global
G
symmetry is in modern jargon referred to as an
invertible global 0-form
symmetry
[
20
]
.

Here and below, for
q=0,1
, a
q-form
operator is a
topological
operator that acts non-trivially only on a codimension q submanifold of the spatial manifold, i.e. the two-dimensional torus. The case of the
\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}}u_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}
symmetry operators then naturally corresponds to
q=0
.

For the sake of being concrete we will henceforth make an explicit choice of local Hilbert space and its representation.
2
2

2

It should be noted that the gauging procedure which follows can be carried out for any on-site realization of the symmetry
[
13
]
. However, in the construction of the emergent state below, the choice of the representation of the G symmetry on the boundary does not influence the bulk stabilizers of the emergent state.
To this end we consider the character group
\widehat{G}:={\rm Hom}(G,\rm U(1))
of
G
, which is isomorphic to
G
here since
G
is abelian. We then choose the local Hilbert space as
\mathcal{H}^{\mathsf{v}}=\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]
where
\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]:={\rm Span}_{\mathbb{C}}\{\ket{\chi}|\chi\in\widehat{G}\}
is endowed with the inner product
\innerproduct{\chi_1}{\chi_2}=\delta_{\chi_{1},\chi_{2}}
. This local Hilbert space is then assumed to carry the
G
-representation
u_{g}=Z_{g}
defined as
Z_{g}:=\sum_{\chi\in\widehat{G}}\chi(g)\outerproduct{\chi}{\chi}
,
\forall g\in G
. Let us also introduce the shorthand
\mathbb{U}_{g}:=\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)}Z^{\mathsf{v}}_{g}
.

1.1
Review: gauging two-dimensional abelian 0-form symmetries

Gauging a global on-site 0-form
G
symmetry à la
[
13
]
3
3

3

Notice that the framework of
[
13
]
applies more generally to non-abelian groups as well. The gauged theory in that case enjoys Wilson loop symmetries labeled by representations of the symmetry group. Wilson loops corresponding to higher-dimensional representations of the group can be realized on the lattice by non-trivial
matrix product operators

[
21
,
22
,
23
]
.
begins with supplementing the Hilbert space with gauge degrees of freedom supported on the edges
\mathsf{E}(\Lambda)
and valued in
\mathbb{C}[G]:={\rm Span}_{\mathbb{C}}\{\ket{g}|g\in G\}
,
\innerproduct{g_1}{g_2}=\delta_{g_{1},g_{2}}
. The group algebra
\mathbb{C}[G]
is naturally endowed with the left regular representation given by:

X_{g}:=\sum_{h\in G}\outerproduct{gh}{h},\quad\forall g\in G.

(1.2)

On this enlarged Hilbert space

\left(\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)}\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]\right)\otimes\left(\bigotimes_{\mathsf{e}\in\mathsf{E}(\Lambda)}\mathbb{C}[G]\right)

(1.3)

we then define a
gauge transformation
for every vertex
\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)
and every
g\in G
:

\mathcal{G}_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}:=Z_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}\,\bigotimes_{\mathsf{e}(\rightarrow\mathsf{v})}\,X_{\bar{g}}^{\mathsf{e}}\,\bigotimes_{\mathsf{e}(\leftarrow\mathsf{v})}\,X_{g}^{\mathsf{e}}\ .

(1.4)

Here,
\mathsf{e}(\rightarrow\!\mathsf{v})
, respectively
\mathsf{e}(\leftarrow\!\mathsf{v})
, stands for the set of edges of
\Lambda
that point into, respectively point away from, the fixed vertex
\mathsf{v}
.

Notice that the operators
\mathcal{G}_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}
in
form a
local
representation of
G
in the sense that they are supported on a small neighborhood around
\mathsf{v}
and obey
\mathcal{G}_{g_{1}}^{\mathsf{v}}\cdot\mathcal{G}_{g_{2}}^{\mathsf{v}}=\mathcal{G}_{g_{1}g_{2}}^{\mathsf{v}}
for every
\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)
and for every
g_{1},g_{2}\in G
. Moreover, notice that the global symmetry operators are recovered by taking the product of the local symmetry operators on all vertices, namely

\prod_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)}\mathcal{G}^{\mathsf{v}}_{g}=\mathbb{U}_{g},\quad\forall g\in G.

(1.5)

Next, a
local
projector is obtained by averaging
\mathcal{G}_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}
over
G
:

\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{v}}:=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\mathcal{G}_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}.

(1.6)

Indeed it is straightforward to verify that
\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{v}}\cdot\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{v}}=\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{v}}
,
\forall\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)
by a relabeling of summation variables.

The commutation of the local projectors
\big[\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{v}},\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{v}^{\prime}}\big]=0
allows us to unambiguously define the
global
projector onto the gauge invariant subspace of the enlarged Hilbert space:

\mathcal{P}:=\prod_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)}\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{v}}.

(1.7)

The state
\ket{\psi}
is then gauged by applying the projector
\mathcal{P}
to the initial state
\ket{\psi}
coupled to a trivial flat gauge field
\bigotimes_{\mathsf{e}\in\mathsf{E}(\Lambda)}\ket{1}^{\mathsf{e}}
. Hence, we define the
gauging map

\mathcal{G}^{0}
for the global 0-form
G
symmetry as:

\displaystyle\mathcal{G}^{0}:=\mathcal{P}\bigg(\bigotimes_{\mathsf{e}\in\mathsf{E}(\Lambda)}\ket{1}^{\mathsf{e}}\bigg)\,:

(1.8)

\displaystyle\,\bigg(\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)}\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]\bigg)\rightarrow\bigg(\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)}\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]\bigg)\otimes\bigg(\bigotimes_{\mathsf{e}\in\mathsf{E}(\Lambda)}\mathbb{C}[G]\bigg),

and the
gauged state
is by definition
\mathcal{G}^{0}\ket{\psi}
.

In order to elucidate the above procedure and facilitate the construction of the emergent state below, let us present a tensor network representation of the gauging map
\mathcal{G}^{0}
. To this end we introduce two types of tensors. For every vertex of the lattice with
m
incoming edges and
n
outgoing edges, we introduce the rank-
(m+n)

vertex tensor
, or
Z-type tensor
, defined as follows:

{\scriptstyle Z}

\displaystyle:=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\chi_{1},\chi_{2}\\

(1.12)

where the orientation of the horizontal red legs is assumed to be in correspondence with the orientation of the edges of the lattice. Note that the commutation of two local projectors
\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{v}},\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{v}^{\prime}}
on different vertices
\mathsf{v}\neq\mathsf{v}^{\prime}
follows immediately from the definition of the +-type tensors. Combining this observation with the fact that projecting one of the incoming legs of the +-type tensor
onto
\ket{1}
effectively removes that leg, it follows that the gauging map
\mathcal{G}^{0}
admits a representation as projected entangled-pair operator (PEPO) of bond dimension
|G|
, whose unit cell can be depicted as:

(1.13)

In this construction it should be understood that the full PEPO on the torus is obtained by placing copies of this unit cell on all vertices of the lattice and contracting along the virtual red legs according to the connectivity of the lattice.

Let us proceed by dissecting the symmetry properties of the gauging map
\mathcal{G}^{0}
. One of the upshots of the PEPO representation is that these symmetry properties automatically follow from the symmetry properties of the local tensors from which the PEPO is made up. It follows readily from its definition that the vertex tensor satisfies

(1.15)

Consider first gauge invariance of the gauging map, that is
\mathcal{G}^{\mathsf{v}}_{g}\cdot\mathcal{G}^{0}=\mathcal{G}^{0}
for all
g\in G
and
\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\square)
. Note that it is exactly in this sense that this gauging procedure
localizes
the global 0-form
G
symmetry.

From the PEPO representation this property can be deduced by combining the second relation in
with both identities in
and noticing that all
X_{g}^{(\dagger)}
’s on the virtual level exactly cancel with each other. Note that algebraically this follows directly from a renaming of summation variable in the definition of
\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{v}}

. One also has that
\mathcal{G}^{0}\cdot\mathbb{U}_{g}=\mathcal{G}^{0}
for all
g\in G
. Physically this means that the gauging map projects out states which transform non-trivially under the global symmetry
G
. As such,
\mathcal{G}^{0}
has a non-trivial kernel spanned by states in the original matter Hilbert space
\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)}\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]
which are charged under the
G
symmetry. This can be seen from application of the first identity in
on every vertex together with the invariance of the edge tensors, namely

(1.16)

which is deduced from
.

As mentioned in the introduction, the gauged states exhibit at least a global 1-form
\widehat{G}
symmetry as a consequence of the imposed Gauss laws. This 1-form symmetry is the topic of the next section.

To conclude this paragraph, a comment which is of importance for what follows is in place. As argued in
[
13
]
it is possible to disentangle the initial matter degrees of freedom from the newly introduced gauge degrees of freedom by means of a finite depth unitary quantum circuit, rendering the Gauss constraints
\mathcal{G}_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}\overset{!}{=}1
trivial and effectively freezing the matter degrees of freedom to the
+1
eigenstate of
Z_{g}
. As showcased below, we will construct a three-dimensional state by concatenating gauging operators, wherein the ‘matter’ degrees of freedom in every layer will play the role of physical degrees of freedom of the three-dimensional state. We therefore refrain from applying this unitary circuit.

1.2
The dual 1-form symmetry

Let us consider
\ell\in Z_{1}(\Lambda,\mathbb{Z})
to be an oriented closed path supported on the edges of the lattice
\Lambda
, and introduce

Z_{\chi}:=\sum_{g\in G}\chi(g)\outerproduct{g}{g},\quad\forall\chi\in\widehat{G},

(1.17)

which together with
X_{g}
obeys the following commutation relation:

Z_{\chi}X_{g}=\chi(g)\,X_{g}Z_{\chi}.

(1.18)

We define then following
Wilson loop
operators acting exclusively on the gauge degrees of freedom:

\mathbb{U}_{\chi}[\ell]:=\bigotimes_{\mathsf{e}\in\ell}Z_{o_{\ell}^{\mathsf{e}}(\chi)}^{\mathsf{e}}.

(1.19)

Here,
o_{\ell}^{\mathsf{e}}(\chi)
is defined so that
o_{\ell}^{\mathsf{e}}(\chi)=\chi
if the orientation of
\mathsf{e}
and
\ell
coincide and
\bar{\chi}
otherwise. As we will momentarily show, it holds that

\mathbb{U}_{\chi}[\ell]\cdot\mathcal{G}^{0}=\mathcal{G}^{0},

(1.20)

\forall\chi\in\widehat{G},\ell\in Z_{1}(\Lambda,\mathbb{Z})
. This implies that the gauged state
\mathcal{G}^{0}\ket{\psi}
transforms trivially under
\mathbb{U}_{\chi}[\ell]
for every valid choice of
\ell
and every character
\chi\in\widehat{G}
. Making use of the fact that

\chi_{1}(g)\chi_{2}(g)=(\chi_{1}\otimes\chi_{2})(g),

(1.21)

\forall\chi_{1},\chi_{2}\in\widehat{G},g\in G,
it follows that the operators
\mathbb{U}_{\chi}[\ell]
, with same
\ell
, multiply according to the product of characters in
\widehat{G}
, i.e.:

\mathbb{U}_{\chi_{1}}[\ell]\cdot\mathbb{U}_{\chi_{2}}[\ell]=\mathbb{U}_{\chi_{1}\otimes\chi_{2}}[\ell].

(1.22)

Also note that the operators
\mathbb{U}_{\chi}[\ell]
are invariant under continuous deformations of
\ell
, rendering them
topological
. These observations demonstrate that after gauging a global 0-form
G
symmetry, a
global 1-form
\widehat{G}
symmetry emerges.
4
4

4

In fact, one should think of the emergent 1-form
\widehat{G}
symmetry, or more precisely
{\rm Rep}(G)
symmetry, as being the invertible component of the full symmetry structure of the gauge theory. The complete symmetry structure was shown to constitute the 1-form symmetry together with all its 0-form
condensation descendants
and is organized in the
fusion 2-category

2{\rm Rep}(G)

[
24
,
25
,
26
,
27
,
23
,
28
]
.

) as a
kinematical
constraint satisfied by all allowed states in the gauge invariant Hilbert space.

(1.24)

Both these invariance properties once more follow directly from the definitions of these respective tensors. From them, the claim
follows readily as again all occurrences of
Z_{\chi}^{(\dagger)}
that appear on the virtual level after application of
\mathbb{U}_{\chi}[\ell]
cancel.

For the sake of completeness, let us also verify this more explicitly algebraically. To this end, one checks that for every such loop
\ell
this line operator commutes with the local gauge transformations:

\mathbb{U}_{\chi}[\ell]\cdot\mathcal{G}_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}=\mathcal{G}_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}\cdot\mathbb{U}_{\chi}[\ell],\quad\forall g\in G,\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda).

(1.25)

To prove this, first notice that if
\mathbb{U}_{\chi}[\ell]
and
\mathcal{G}_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}
overlap, they overlap in an even number of edges. Let us consider just the case of two overlapping edges that we call
\mathsf{e}_{1}
,
\mathsf{e}_{2}
. Then for the given vertex
\mathsf{v}
, if both
\mathsf{e}_{1}
,
\mathsf{e}_{2}
have the same orientation as
\ell
or both have the opposite orientation as
\ell
, commuting
\mathbb{U}_{\chi}[\ell]
through
\mathcal{G}_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}
yields two cancelling phases
\chi(g)
and
\bar{\chi}(g)
by virtue of the definition of
\mathcal{G}_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}
and
. If on the other hand
\ell
has the same orientation as
\mathsf{e}_{1}
but has the opposite orientation as
\mathsf{e}_{2}
, then we also obtain, due to the relative difference in orientation, phases
\chi(g)
and
\bar{\chi}(g)
that cancel. From
together with the fact that

\mathbb{U}_{\chi}[\ell]\big(\bigotimes_{\mathsf{e}\in\mathsf{E}(\Lambda)}\ket{1}^{\mathsf{e}}\big)=\bigotimes_{\mathsf{e}\in\mathsf{E}(\Lambda)}\ket{ 1}^{\mathsf{e}}

(1.26)

we can conclude
.

1.3
Gauging the dual 1-form symmetry

Since the emergent 1-form symmetry is realized on-site, it is anomaly-free in the sense of
[
29
]
and can hence be gauged. To this end we use a similar procedure as in
[
13
,
19
,
14
]
. After gauging this 1-form symmetry one expects the original 0-form
G
symmetry to re-emerge
[
20
,
19
]
.

Following
[
19
,
14
,
30
]
, gauging of the 1-form symmetry happens via introduction of gauge degrees of freedom on the
vertices

\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)
of the lattice valued in the group algebra
\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]
.
5
5

5

By invoking a form of Poincaré duality, one can identify the vertices of the primal lattice
\Lambda
with the plaquettes of the dual lattice
\Lambda^{\vee}
, i.e.
\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)\equiv\mathsf{P}(\Lambda^{\vee})
. In that sense the gauge field can indeed be thought of as a
2-form gauge field
for the global 1-form symmetry
[
30
]
.
A local
1-form gauge transformation
for every edge
\mathsf{e}\in\mathsf{E}(\Lambda)
is then constructed as follows:

\mathcal{G}^{\mathsf{e}}_{\chi}:=X_{\chi}^{\mathsf{v}(\leftarrow\mathsf{e})}\otimes Z_{\chi}^{\mathsf{e}}\otimes X_{\bar{\chi}}^{\mathsf{v}(\rightarrow\mathsf{e})},

(1.27)

where we used an analogue notation to the one in
denoting by
\mathsf{v}(\leftarrow\!\mathsf{e})
the vertex which is the target of
\mathsf{e}
and by
\mathsf{v}(\rightarrow\!\mathsf{e})
the source vertex of the edge
\mathsf{e}
. Naturally,
X_{\chi}
is defined as

X_{\chi}:=\sum_{\eta\in\widehat{G}}\outerproduct{\chi\eta}{\eta}.

(1.28)

Akin to the case of the gauging of a global 0-form symmetry, these operators form a
local
representation of
\widehat{G}
supported near
\mathsf{e}
,
\mathcal{G}^{\mathsf{e}}_{\chi_{1}}\cdot\mathcal{G}^{\mathsf{e}}_{\chi_{2}}=\mathcal{G}^{\mathsf{e}}_{\chi_{1}\chi_{2}}
,
\forall\chi_{1},\chi_{2}\in\widehat{G}
. Notice that the global 1-form symmetries can be recovered by taking the (oriented) product of the 1-form gauge transformations along the loop
\ell
, i.e.:

\mathbb{U}_{\chi}[\ell]=\prod_{\mathsf{e}\in\ell}\mathcal{G}^{\mathsf{e}}_{o_{\ell}^{\mathsf{e}}(\chi)},

(1.29)

\forall\chi\in\widehat{G},\ \ell\in Z_{1}(\Lambda,\mathbb{Z})
, analogous to
.

Group-averaging over
\widehat{G}
allows us to construct the local projectors

\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{e}}:=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{\chi\in\widehat{G}}\mathcal{G}_{\chi}^{\mathsf{e}},

(1.30)

where we made use of
|G|=|\widehat{G}|
. From these we can again unambiguously construct the global projector onto the gauge invariant subspace as:

\mathcal{P}:=\prod_{\mathsf{e}\in\mathsf{E}(\Lambda)}\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{e}}.

(1.31)

Gauging the 1-form symmetry then ultimately happens in a similar fashion as in the 0-form case. We construct a gauging map by initializing all newly introduced gauge degrees of freedom in the trivial representation
\underline{1}\in\widehat{G}
followed by acting with the projector onto the gauge invariant subspace:

\displaystyle\mathcal{G}^{1}:=\mathcal{P}\bigg(\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)}\ket{\ul 1}^{\mathsf{e}}\bigg)\,:

(1.32)

\displaystyle\bigg(\bigotimes_{\mathsf{e}\in\mathsf{E}(\Lambda)}\mathbb{C}[G]\bigg)\rightarrow\bigg(\bigotimes_{\mathsf{e}\in\mathsf{E}(\Lambda)}\mathbb{C}[G]\bigg)\otimes\bigg(\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)}\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]\bigg).

Let us draw attention to the fact that without loss of generality the gauging map
\mathcal{G}^{1}
has as its domain only the edge degrees of freedom. This can be traced back to the fact that the emergent 1-form symmetry generators
\mathbb{U}_{\chi}[\ell]
only act (non-trivially) on these degrees of freedom.

Let us now proceed by showcasing the tensor network representation of the gauging map
\mathcal{G}^{1}
, and its symmetry properties. In a similar vein as for the gauging map of the global 0-form
G
symmetry, we introduce tensors that will be placed on the edges of the lattice that read:

(1.39)

This is not an independent property as it can be derived immediately from
.

Finally and crucially, after gauging the 1-form symmetry the initial global 0-form
G
symmetry reappears as anticipated. Indeed, it is found that

\mathbb{U}_{g}\cdot\mathcal{G}^{1}=\mathcal{G}^{1},

(1.40)

for all
g\in G
.

For future reference we demonstrate this here algebraically. To this end, first note that for two vertices
\mathsf{v},\mathsf{v}^{\prime}
which share an edge
\mathsf{e}
,
Z_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}\otimes Z_{g}^{\mathsf{v}^{\prime}}
commutes with the gauge transformation
\mathcal{G}^{\mathsf{e}}_{\chi}
,
\forall g\in G
by virtue of the identity

Z_{g}X_{\chi}=\chi(g)X_{\chi}Z_{g}.

(1.41)

Combined with the observation that

\mathbb{U}_{g}\big(\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)}\ket{1}^{\mathsf{v}}\big)=\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)}\ket{1}^{\mathsf{v}},

(1.42)

we recover indeed
.

In order to verify this using the PEPO representation
on the other hand, the relevant invariance properties this time read:

(1.44)

From these properties,
follows readily since after application of
\mathbb{U}_{g}
on the gauging map, all occurrences of
Z_{g}^{(\dagger)}
again cancel on the virtual bonds.

1.4
3D local symmetries from iterative gauging

Constructing a three-dimensional state from the above gauging maps now happens as follows. We start by choosing a two-dimensional state
\ket{\psi}
that will serve as the boundary condition of the three-dimensional state and fixing a choice of abelian group
G
. We assume, as anticipated above, that this state lives in
\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)}\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]
and transforms trivially under the abelian 0-form
G
symmetry
\mathbb{U}_{g}
, i.e.
\mathbb{U}_{g}\ket{\psi}=\ket{\psi}
,
\forall g\in G
. Throughout the above discussions
\Lambda
was kept completely general, and as such the construction that follows also can be applied to this most general case.

On
\ket{\psi}
we can thus first act with the gauging operator
\mathcal{G}^{0}
defined explicitly in
, thereby introducing degrees of freedom valued in
\mathbb{C}[G]
and supported on the edges of
\Lambda
. Indeed, recall that
\mathcal{G}^{0}
acts according to
\mathcal{G}^{0}:\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]^{\otimes\mathsf{V}}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]^{\otimes\mathsf{V}}\otimes\mathbb{C}[G]^{\otimes\mathsf{E}}
, in which
\otimes\mathsf{E}
and
\otimes\mathsf{V}
stand for tensor products over the vertices and edges of the lattice. The gauged state
\mathcal{G}^{0}\ket{\psi}
has then as argued in
an emergent dual 1-form
\widehat{G}
symmetry which is completely supported on the edges of
\Lambda
and that in turn can be gauged using the procedure outlined in
. Notice that the gauging map for this 1-form symmetry,
\mathcal{G}^{1}
defined in (
), acts only on the
\mathbb{C}[G]
-valued degrees of freedom supported on the edges, leaving the original ‘matter’ degrees of freedom on the vertices
\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)
valued in
\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]
untouched. With slight abuse of notation:
\mathcal{G}^{1}:\mathbb{C}[G]^{\otimes\mathsf{E}}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}[G]^{\otimes\mathsf{E}}\otimes\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]^{\otimes\mathsf{V}}
. In turn we can then again gauge the emergent 0-form
G
symmetry that arises after the application of
\mathcal{G}^{1}
using the gauging map
\mathcal{G}^{0}
. In this step
\mathcal{G}^{0}
does not act on the degrees of freedom in
\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]
living on
\mathsf{E}(\Lambda)
. By repeatedly concatenating the gauging maps
\mathcal{G}^{0}
and
\mathcal{G}^{1}
we thus in every step are left with degrees of freedom in
\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]
and
\mathbb{C}[G]
which are not acted upon by the next gauging map. These are the degrees of freedom which, following the paradigm of Ref.
[
12
]
, are interpreted as
physical
degrees of freedom of a
foliated
three-dimensional state
\ket{\Psi[\psi]}
whose 2D layers are made up of the ‘matter’ degrees of freedom in every application of the gauging maps. Formally
\ket{\Psi[\psi]}
reads:

\ket{\Psi[\psi]}:=\cdots\circ\mathcal{G}^{1}_{\mathsf{2}}\circ\mathcal{G}^{0}_{\mathsf{\frac{3}{2}}}\circ\mathcal{G}^{1}_{\mathsf{1}}\circ\mathcal{G}^{0}_{\mathsf{\frac{1}{2}}}\ket{\psi}.

(1.45)

The exact meaning of the subscripts will be explained momentarily.

For concreteness we specialize to the square lattice
\square=\Lambda
henceforth. It can then be argued that the physical degrees of freedom of
\ket{\Psi[\psi]}
naturally organize themselves on the edges of a three-dimensional cubic lattice that we will denote by
, and where the initial two-dimensional state serves as a physical boundary of the lattice.

We therefore consider the cubic lattice as being made up of alternating layers of vertical edges followed by a layer of horizontal edges, that we label by
{\mathsf{\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2}},\dots}
and
\mathsf{1,2},\dots
respectively. The cubic lattice hence has a physical boundary made up of vertical edges.

For every layer of vertical edges we associate these edges with the vertices of a copy of
\square
and the corresponding
\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]
-valued ‘matter’ degrees of freedom that are not acted upon by the gauging maps
\mathcal{G}^{1}
. Analogously, we associate with every horizontal edge the
\mathbb{C}[G]
-valued degrees of freedom that are untouched by the
\mathcal{G}^{0}
’s.

Using a
blue
color for edges that carry a copy of the local Hilbert space
\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]
and
red
for those with a copy of
\mathbb{C}[G]
, one can depict the cubic lattice away from the boundary as follows:

(1.47)

In this figure it is understood that all horizontal legs are contracted with neighboring unit cells and the dots represent a contraction with unit cells in the vertical direction. The physical degrees of freedom of the state then correspond to the uncontracted vertical legs.

By virtue of the local symmetries of all the gauging maps appearing in
, the obtained state
\ket{\Psi[\psi]}
also inherits those local symmetries in a slightly modified way. More precisely, the emergent state
\ket{\Psi[\psi]}
is stabilized by plaquette operators for every plaquette of the cubic lattice, coming from the localization of the
1
-form symmetry, and vertex operators for every vertex, from gauging the global
0
-form symmetry. We denote the plaquette stabilizers which are labeled by
\chi\in\widehat{G}
by
\mathbb{b}^{\mathsf{p}}
:

\displaystyle\mathbb{b}^{\mathsf{p}_{xz}}_{\chi}\ket{\Psi[\psi]}

\displaystyle=\ket{\Psi[\psi]},

(1.48)

\displaystyle\mathbb{b}^{\mathsf{p}_{yz}}_{\chi}\ket{\Psi[\psi]}

\displaystyle=\ket{\Psi[\psi]},

(1.49)

\displaystyle\mathbb{b}^{\mathsf{p}_{xy}}_{\chi}\ket{\Psi[\psi]}

\displaystyle=\ket{\Psi[\psi]},

(1.50)

and the vertex stabilizers
\mathbb{a}^{\mathsf{v}}
carry a group label
g\in G
:

\mathbb{a}^{\mathsf{v}}_{g}\ket{\Psi[\psi]}=\ket{\Psi[\psi]}.

(1.51)

(1.55)

Let us first show algebraically that
\mathbb{b}^{\mathsf{p}_{xz}}_{\chi}
and
\mathbb{b}^{\mathsf{p}_{yz}}_{\chi}
stabilize
\ket{\Psi[\psi]}
before residing to our graphical PEPO representation of the state. To this end we single out one of those plaquette term. From the commutation relation
together with the definition of
\mathcal{G}^{0}
in terms of the local gauge transformations (
), it follows that

\begin{split}&\big(X_{\chi}^{\mathsf{v}(\leftarrow\mathsf{e})}\otimes Z_{\bar{\chi}}^{\mathsf{e}}\otimes X_{\bar{\chi}}^{\mathsf{v}(\rightarrow\mathsf{e})}\big)\cdot\mathcal{G}^{0}\\
&\hskip 45.0pt=\mathcal{G}^{0}\cdot\big(X_{\chi}^{\mathsf{v}(\leftarrow\mathsf{e})}\otimes X_{\bar{\chi}}^{\mathsf{v}(\rightarrow\mathsf{e})}\big).\end{split}

(1.56)

Recognizing then
X_{\chi}^{\mathsf{v}(\leftarrow\mathsf{e})}\otimes Z_{\chi}\otimes X_{\bar{\chi}}^{\mathsf{v}(\rightarrow\mathsf{e})}
as the local 1-form gauge transformation (
), which leaves
\mathcal{G}^{1}
invariant, together with the fact that
Z_{\bar{\chi}}\cdot\mathcal{G}^{1}=\mathcal{G}^{1}\cdot Z_{\bar{\chi}}
proves that
\mathbb{b}^{\mathsf{p}_{xz}}_{\chi}
and
\mathbb{b}^{\mathsf{p}_{yz}}_{\chi}
are stabilizers of the state.

1.5
Gapped boundary conditions

The local stabilizers analyzed so far act on the bulk of the three-dimensional state
\ket{\Psi[\psi]}
. In this section we study the boundary stabilizers. These naturally are given by a subset of truncated bulk stabilizers commuting with the bulk stabilizers
\mathbb{b}
and
\mathbb{a}
defined above, where the subset depends on the choice of the boundary state
\ket{\psi}
, in particular the way in which
\ket{\psi}
is invariant under the
G
0-form symmetry. Indeed, for every choice of subgroup
H\leq G
one can construct explicitly a
G
-symmetric boundary state
\ket{\psi}_{H}
for which
\ket{\Psi[\psi_H]}
is a ground state of the bulk Hamiltonian
\mathbb{H}^{\rm blk}
(
) plus additional boundary terms which are projectors and which all commute with the terms in
\mathbb{H}^{\rm blk}
(
) and among themselves.

(1.69)

These terms commute both with the bulk vertex operators
\mathbb{a}^{\mathsf{v}}_{g}
and plaquette operators
\mathbb{b}^{\mathsf{p}}_{\chi}
. Naturally, they also commute all among each other. From the explicit form of the gauging maps
\mathcal{G}^{0}_{\frac{1}{2}}
and
\mathcal{G}^{1}_{1}
it follows that given an irrep
\chi\in\widehat{G}
the operators (
1.68
-
1.69
) are stabilizers of
\ket{\Psi[\psi]}
if and only if
(X^{\mathsf{v}}_{\bar{\chi}}\otimes X^{\mathsf{v}^{\prime}}_{\chi})\ket{\psi}=\ket{\psi}
, equivalently

\begin{multlined}\mathbb{d}_{\chi}\ket{\Psi[\psi]}=\ket{\Psi[\psi]}\iff\\
\bra{\psi}(X^{\mathsf{v}}_{\bar{\chi}}\otimes X^{\mathsf{v}^{\prime}}_{\chi})\ket{\psi}=1\end{multlined}

(1.70)

for neighboring vertices
\mathsf{v},\mathsf{v}^{\prime}\in\mathsf{V}(\square)
. Notice that
X_{\bar{\chi}}\otimes X_{\chi}
is an order parameter for the (partial) breaking of the global 0-form
G
symmetry. Its expectation value is a two-point symmetric correlation function.

In what follows we show that given a choice of subgroup
H\leq G
,
\mathbb{d}_{\chi}
is a stabilizer of
\ket{\Psi[\psi_H]}
for an appropriate boundary state
\ket{\psi}_{H}
depending on that subgroup, provided that
\chi
is trivial when restricted to
H
. It is a fact that characters in
\widehat{G}
that are trivial when restricted to
H
form a subgroup of
\widehat{G}
isomorphic to
\widehat{G/H}
. From now on we will abuse notation and denote this subgroup simply by
\widehat{G/H}\leq\widehat{G}
. For the chosen subgroup
H\leq G
we then propose following boundary state
\ket{\psi}_{H}
. First, we define the normalized states

\ket{+}_{H}:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|G/H|}}\sum_{[\chi]\in\widehat{G/H}}\ket{\chi}.

(1.71)

Notice that
\ket{+}_{H}
is stabilized by
H
in the sense that
Z_{h}\ket{+}_{H}=\ket{+}_{H}
for all
h\in H
. Given
\ket{+}_{H}
we define

\ket{\psi}_{H}:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|G/H|}}\sum_{[g]\in G/H}\bigg(\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\square)}Z_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}\ket{+}^{\mathsf{v}}_{H}\bigg).

(1.72)

By construction
\ket{\psi}_{H}
is symmetric under the 0-form
G
symmetry and, as anticipated, is symmetric under
\{X^{\mathsf{v}}_{\bar{\chi}}\otimes X^{\mathsf{v}^{\prime}}_{\chi},\chi\in\widehat{G/H}\}
since
X^{\mathsf{v}}_{\chi}
leaves invariant
\ket{+}_{H}
and
X^{\mathsf{v}}_{\bar{\chi}}\otimes X^{\mathsf{v}^{\prime}}_{\chi}
commutes with

(1.82)

Similarly as in the previous case one could define
|\hat{\psi}\rangle_{\widehat{H}}
hosting a (partial) symmetry breaking phase of the 1-form symmetry with unbroken symmetry group
\widehat{H}\leq\widehat{G}
. Commuting boundary stabilizers for such a state are given by

\displaystyle\mathbb{R}_{H}^{\mathsf{v}}

\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{|H|}\sum_{h\in H}\mathbb{e}^{\mathsf{v}}_{h},

(1.83)

\displaystyle\mathbb{R}_{H}^{\mathsf{e}}

\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{|G/H|}\sum_{\chi\in\widehat{G/H}}\mathbb{f}^{\mathsf{e}}_{\chi}.

(1.84)

Notice thus in particular that
|\hat{\psi}\rangle
can host non-trivial 2D topological order. It is understood that besides these boundaries and the
G
symmetry breaking ones considered above, it is also possible to define additional gapped boundaries which amount to (trivially) stacking a 2D topological order or stacking a 2D topological order while condensing composites of boundary anyons of the emergent state and (bulk) anyons from the stacked topological order
[
34
]
.

2
General framework

What are the main takeaways from this introductory example? From iteratively gauging a global abelian 0-form symmetry and its dual 1-form symmetry we obtain stabilizer codes (local commuting projector Hamiltonians) in one dimension higher. Moreover, the obtained codes can be readily extended to include gapped boundary terms, and we have written down the gauging maps and states explicitly in terms of tensor networks.

The goal of this section is to provide a general framework for iteratively gauging a state
\ket{\psi}
which is symmetric under a collection of abelian symmetries defined via certain
check operators
which commute with them. Hereby we extend the formalism of
[
14
]
to arbitrary abelian groups. We argue that in this framework the concatenated gauging maps generically exhibit
local symmetries
originating from the Gauss constraints of the symmetries under scrutiny. These local symmetries can in turn be organized in an
emergent
local commuting projector Hamiltonian that naturally lives in one dimension higher than the initial state
\ket{\psi}
which is being gauged. Towards the end of this section we comment on the inclusion of the boundary terms in the emergent Hamiltonian which can be identified with certain spontaneous symmetry breaking patterns of the boundary symmetry realized by
\ket{\psi}
. Since these gauging maps can be defined in any dimension, we recover the results from
[
12
]
as a specific case.

2.1
Gauging abelian symmetries

To set the scene, we assume a lattice
\Lambda
in which each vertex
\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)
supports a copy of
\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]
. The tensor product Hilbert space
\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)}\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]
will be written as
\mathcal{H}:=\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)}\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]
henceforth. Notice that we don’t make any assumption about the underlying topology or dimension of the spatial manifold on which
\Lambda
is defined.

Throughout this section we deal with symmetry operators that are fully specified by a
complete collection
of
check operators
, labeled
c\in\mathcal{C}
, that commute with all of them. The formal gauging procedure of Williamson
[
14
]
then happens via the introduction of a gauge degree of freedom for every such check. Formally, consider for any
g\in G
the operators

\mathbb{U}_{g}[\Omega]:=\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\Omega}Z_{g}^{\mathsf{v}},\quad g\in G,

(2.1)

where
\Omega
is a subset of the vertices, i.e.
\Omega\subseteq\mathsf{V}(\Omega)
. Borrowing the notation of
[
14
]
, we will denote by
\eta
a function

\begin{split}\eta:\,&\mathcal{C}\rightarrow P(\mathsf{V}(\Lambda))\\
&c\rightarrow\eta(c)\subseteq\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)\end{split}\,\,,

(2.2)

from
\mathcal{C}
to the power set
P(\mathsf{V}(\Lambda))
. Physically,
\eta
maps a given constraint
c
from the collection
\mathcal{C}
, that will below be identified with the gauge degrees of freedom, to a corresponding set of vertices
\eta(c)\subseteq\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)
. Furthermore we introduce the involution
o^{c}_{\mathsf{v}}(\chi)
which evaluates to
\chi
or
\bar{\chi}
depending on the
relative orientation
of the constraint
c
and the vertex
\mathsf{v}
. An operator
\mathbb{U}_{g}[\Omega]
is then a
valid symmetry generator
if it commutes with the checks

X_{\chi}^{c}:=\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\eta(c)}X^{\mathsf{v}}_{o^{c}_{\mathsf{v}}(\chi)}

(2.3)

for all
c\in\mathcal{C}
and all
\chi\in\widehat{G}
. Below, we will sometimes refer to the symmetry structure generated by these valid symmetry generators as the
initial
symmetry.

To connect with the previous section, let us remark that the global 0-form
G
symmetry corresponds to the case
\Omega=\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)
, and thus
\mathbb{U}_{g}[\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)]\equiv\mathbb{U}_{g}
. For these symmetry generators the checks can be chosen so that there is exactly one check per edge of the lattice, i.e.
\mathcal{C}\equiv\mathsf{E}(\Lambda)
. Explicitly, the checks then read
X^{\mathsf{e}}_{\chi}=X^{\mathsf{v}(\rightarrow\mathsf{e})}_{\chi}\otimes X^{\mathsf{v}(\leftarrow\mathsf{e})}_{\bar{\chi}}
, where we refer to the previous section for a detailed explanation of the notation.

An important observation is that the local constraints can be interpreted as local Hamiltonian terms that commute with the symmetry
[
14
]
. As such, they can be used to construct
generalized Ising models
and when perturbed, for example with single-vertex
Z_{g}
terms, they host symmetry breaking phases of such symmetries.

We now proceed by gauging the symmetry generated by the operators
\mathbb{U}_{g}[\Omega]
, essentially mimicking the procedure used in the previous section based on
[
13
,
14
]
adapted to this more general setting. To this end we first enlarge the ‘matter’ Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}
with a
\mathbb{C}[G]
-valued
gauge degree of freedom
for every check in
\mathcal{C}
. We will denote the physical support of the gauge degrees of freedom by
\mathsf{c}\in\mathsf{C}(\Lambda)
where it has to be understood that there is bijection between
\mathsf{C}(\Lambda)
and
\mathcal{C}
. Typically,
\mathsf{C}(\Lambda)
can be identified with a (subset) of k-cells of the lattice
\Lambda
rendering the aforementioned bijection canonical.

Having again the example from the previous section in mind,
\mathsf{C}(\Lambda)
can thus be identified with
\mathsf{E}(\Lambda)
as anticipated above.

Writing
\widehat{\mathcal{H}}:=\bigotimes_{\mathsf{c}\in\mathcal{C}}\mathbb{C}[G]
, the first step of the gauging procedure thus entails enlarging
\mathcal{H}
according to
\mathcal{H}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}\otimes\widehat{\mathcal{H}}
. Given the map
\eta
defined above, we define
\eta^{-1}(\mathsf{v})
as the preimage of
\mathsf{v}
under
\eta
. In other words,
\eta^{-1}
maps the matter degree of freedom localized on
\mathsf{v}
to its associated gauge degrees of freedom. In light of the above identification of gauge degrees of freedom and constraints, we will also interpret the set of constraints
\eta^{-1}(\mathsf{v})
as its corresponding subset of
\mathsf{C}(\Lambda)
. For every
g\in G
we then define the
gauge transformation

\mathcal{G}_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}
on the enlarged Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}\otimes\widehat{\mathcal{H}}
as:

\mathcal{G}_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}:=Z_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}\bigotimes_{\mathsf{c}\in\eta^{-1}(\mathsf{v})}X^{\mathsf{c}}_{o^{c}_{\mathsf{v}}(g)}.

(2.4)

Out of these gauge transformations, a
local projector
is constructed by taking the
G
-average:

\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{v}}:=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\mathcal{G}_{g}^{\mathsf{v}},

(2.5)

\forall\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)
. Indeed remark that from a redefinition of summation variables it follows that
\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{v}}\cdot\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{v}}=\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{v}}
for all
\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)
.

The
gauging map
is then finally defined as the operator obtained by acting with the local projectors on the trivial gauge field
\bigotimes_{\mathsf{c}\in\mathsf{C}(\Lambda)}\ket{1}^{\mathsf{c}}
:

\begin{gathered}\mathcal{G}:=\bigg(\prod_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)}\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{v}}\bigg)\bigg(\bigotimes_{\mathsf{c}\in\mathsf{C}(\Lambda)}\ket{1}^{\mathsf{c}}\bigg)\,:\\
\mathcal{H}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}\otimes\widehat{\mathcal{H}}.\end{gathered}

(2.6)

Let us summarize the most important properties of
\mathcal{G}
before proceeding. We refer to
[
14
]
for a more detailed digression. For a given
\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)
, the gauge transformations
\mathcal{G}_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}
form by construction a
G
-representation supported on
\eta^{-1}(\mathsf{v})
. It then follows from the definitions that
\mathcal{G}^{\mathsf{v}}_{g}\cdot\mathcal{G}=\mathcal{G}
. By a relabeling of summation variable in the definition of
\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{v}}
it also follows immediately that
\mathcal{G}\cdot\mathbb{U}_{g}[\Omega]=\mathcal{G}
for all allowed symmetry operators. As illustrated in
this property implies that only states
\ket{\psi}
transforming trivially under the symmetry, i.e.
\mathbb{U}_{g}[\Omega]\ket{\psi}=\ket{\psi}
,
\forall g\in G
and for all allowed
\Omega
, are
gaugeable
. Given such a state, we coin
\mathcal{G}\ket{\psi}
the
gauged state
. From
\mathcal{G}^{\mathsf{v}}_{g}\cdot\mathcal{G}=\mathcal{G}
it readily follows that the gauged state is gauge invariant as expected. Even though we only deal with gauging
states
throughout this manuscript, it should be noted that also operators can be gauged using this prescription. In particular,
local
and
symmetric
operators in the initial matter theory are mapped to
dual
local gauge invariant operators under the gauging procedure in such a way that the matrix elements of these symmetric operators w.r.t. a symmetric state are preserved.

As an example, consider once more the case of a 0-form symmetry. Notice that with the choices of relative orientations
o^{\mathsf{e}}_{\mathsf{v}}
implicitly defined above, we recover the Gauss constraints defined above in
, from which eventually the gauging map given in
of
[
13
]
is recovered.

Crucially, the gauge theory obtained via the aforementioned proposal exhibits global
emergent
symmetries that, by construction, are anomaly-free and hence gaugeable
[
29
]
. Let us continue by identifying these emergent symmetries. First notice that even though the constraints
X_{\chi}^{c}
do not commute with the gauging map, the
dressed constraints

Z_{\chi}^{\mathsf{c}}\otimes X^{c}_{\chi}
do commute with all Gauss operators
\mathcal{G}^{\mathsf{v}}_{g}
and, a fortiori, with the gauging map
\mathcal{G}
. Indeed, this follows from a direct computation. For fixed
\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)
and
c\in\mathcal{C}
let us assume without loss of generality that
\mathsf{v}\in\eta(c)
, which necessarily implies that
\mathsf{c}\in\eta^{-1}(\mathsf{v})
:

\displaystyle\bigg(Z_{\chi}^{\mathsf{c}}\otimes X^{c}_{\chi}\bigg)\cdot\mathcal{G}_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}

\displaystyle=\,\,\bigg(Z^{\mathsf{c}}_{\chi}\bigotimes_{\mathsf{w}\in\eta(c)}X^{\mathsf{w}}_{o^{c}_{\mathsf{w}}(\chi)}\bigg)\cdot\bigg(Z_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}\bigotimes_{\mathsf{d}\in\eta^{-1}(\mathsf{v})}X^{\mathsf{d}}_{o^{d}_{\mathsf{v}}(g)}\bigg)

\displaystyle=\,\,o^{c}_{\mathsf{v}}(\bar{\chi})(g)\,\cdot\,\chi(o^{c}_{\mathsf{v}}(g))\cdot\mathcal{G}_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}\cdot\bigg(Z_{\chi}^{\mathsf{c}}\otimes X^{c}_{\chi}\bigg)

\displaystyle=\,\,\mathcal{G}_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}\cdot\bigg(Z_{\chi}^{\mathsf{c}}\otimes X^{c}_{\chi}\bigg).

(2.7)

In the second line the definition of
X^{c}_{\chi}
and
\mathcal{G}_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}
was employed. In the third line we used the commutation relations
and
. Combined with the fact that
Z^{\mathsf{c}}_{\chi}
evaluates to
1
on the trivial gauge field
\bigotimes_{\mathsf{c}\in\mathsf{C}(\Lambda)}\ket{1}^{\mathsf{c}}
, this implies that the constraint
X^{c}_{\chi}
for every
c
and
\chi\in\widehat{G}
is the preimage of
Z^{\mathsf{c}}_{\chi}\otimes X^{c}_{\chi}
under the gauging map
\mathcal{G}
. In particular, it follows that for a choice of constraints
\Gamma\subseteq\mathcal{C}
and choice of involution
\hat{o}^{c}(\chi)
,
c\in\Gamma
such that

\prod_{c\in\Gamma}X_{\hat{o}^{c}(\chi)}^{c}={\rm id},

(2.8)

there exists a corresponding operator in the gauge theory

\mathbb{U}[\Gamma,\hat{o}^{c}]=\prod_{\mathsf{c}\in\Gamma}Z^{\mathsf{c}}_{\hat{o}^{c}(\chi)}

(2.9)

which is an emergent symmetry of
\mathcal{G}
in the sense that

\mathbb{U}[\Gamma,\hat{o}^{c}]\cdot\mathcal{G}=\mathcal{G}.

(2.10)

Applying the above to the example of
\mathcal{G}^{0}
(
) considered in
, we note that
is exactly satisfied for any choice
\Gamma
which coincides with a closed loop
\ell
supported on the edges
\mathsf{E}(\Lambda)
of the lattice. With the above choice of
o^{c}_{\mathsf{v}}
,
\hat{o}^{c}
exactly takes the relative orientation of
\ell
with respect to the orientation of the edges into account.

In order to gauge the emergent symmetry operators we adapt a similar approach as for the initial symmetry (
). Notice that the symmetry generators defined in
commute with the local checks

X^{v}_{g}:=\bigotimes_{\mathsf{c}\in\eta^{-1}(\mathsf{v})}X^{\mathsf{c}}_{o^{c}_{\mathsf{v}}(g)}

(2.11)

which are naturally localized around the vertices
\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)
. Therefore we will identify the set of these checks with the set of vertices
\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)
. To prove that these checks indeed commute with the emergent symmetry generators, consider some vertex
\mathsf{v}\in\eta(\Gamma)
. The identity (
) guarantees the existence of constraints
c,d\in\eta^{-1}(\mathsf{v})
such that
\hat{o}^{c}(o^{c}_{\mathsf{v}}(\chi))=\overline{\hat{o}^{d}(o^{d}_{\mathsf{v}}(\chi))}
. It follows immediately that
Z^{\mathsf{c}}_{\hat{o}^{\mathsf{c}}(\chi)}\otimes Z^{\mathsf{d}}_{\hat{o}^{d}(\chi)}
commutes with
X^{\mathsf{c}}_{o^{c}_{\mathsf{v}}(g)}\otimes X^{\mathsf{d}}_{o^{d}_{\mathsf{v}}(g)}
, from which the claim follows. In order to define the corresponding dual gauging map
\widehat{\mathcal{G}}
, we once more enlarge the Hilbert space according to
\widehat{\mathcal{H}}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathcal{H}}\otimes\mathcal{H}
, on which we define the Gauss operators

\mathcal{G}^{\mathsf{c}}_{\chi}:=Z^{\mathsf{c}}_{\chi}\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\eta(c)}X^{\mathsf{v}}_{\bar{o}^{c}_{\mathsf{v}}(\chi)}.

(2.12)

Notice the complex conjugate appearing in
\bar{o}^{c}_{\mathsf{v}}
. Corresponding local projectors localized around
\mathsf{c}
follow from averaging over
\widehat{G}
:

\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{c}}:=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{\chi\in\widehat{G}}\mathcal{G}^{\mathsf{c}}_{\chi}

(2.13)

Ultimately the dual gauging map reads

\widehat{\mathcal{G}}:=\bigg(\prod_{\mathsf{c}\in\mathsf{C}(\Lambda)}\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{c}}\bigg)\bigg(\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)}\ket{\underline 1}^{\mathsf{v}}\bigg).

(2.14)

It follows that after gauging these emergent symmetries using the gauging map
\widehat{\mathcal{G}}
the original
G
symmetry is recovered, as expected. This is quickly demonstrated by noticing that all symmetry generators
\mathbb{U}_{g}[\Omega]
commute by definition with the checks
X^{c}_{\chi}
, and by extension with the Gauss constraints
\mathcal{G}^{\mathsf{c}}_{\chi}
, so that
\mathbb{U}_{g}[\Omega]\cdot\widehat{\mathcal{G}}=\widehat{\mathcal{G}}
.

Finalizing the example of the previous section, one verifies immediately that the 1-form Gauss constraints
coincide precisely with the definition provided in
applied to the case at hand.

2.2
Concatenation of gauging maps

Let us now consider the composition of the gauging operators defined above. With slight abuse of notation we consider in this section thus the composed operators

\begin{gathered}\widehat{\mathcal{G}}\circ\mathcal{G}:\\
\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]^{\otimes|\mathsf{V}|}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]^{\otimes|\mathsf{V}|}\otimes\mathbb{C}[G]^{\otimes|\mathsf{C}|}\otimes\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]^{\otimes|\mathsf{V}|}\end{gathered}\ ,

and

\begin{gathered}\mathcal{G}\circ\widehat{\mathcal{G}}:\\
\mathbb{C}[G]^{\otimes|\mathsf{C}|}\rightarrow\mathbb{C}[G]^{\otimes|\mathsf{C}|}\otimes\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]^{\otimes|\mathsf{V}|}\otimes\mathbb{C}[G]^{\otimes|\mathsf{C}|}\end{gathered}\ .

Herein,
|\mathsf{V}|
stands for the number of vertices of the lattice
\Lambda
and by definition
|\mathsf{C}|
is equal to the number of constraints defining the initial symmetry (
), i.e.
|\mathsf{C}|=|\mathcal{C}|
. As anticipated above, these concatenated gauging maps exhibit local symmetries that can be traced back to the Gauss constraints enforced by
\mathcal{G}
and
\widehat{\mathcal{G}}
. Crucial in the derivation of the local symmetries are following identities which can be derived in a similar fashion as
eq.

2.7
:

\begin{multlined}\bigg(Z_{\bar{g}}^{\mathsf{v}}\,\bigotimes_{c\in\eta^{-1}(\mathsf{v})}X_{o^{c}_{\mathsf{v}}(g)}^{\mathsf{c}}\bigg)\cdot\widehat{\mathcal{G}}\\
=\widehat{\mathcal{G}}\cdot\bigg(\bigotimes_{c\in\eta^{-1}(\mathsf{v})}\,X_{o^{c}_{\mathsf{v}}(g)}^{\mathsf{c}}\bigg),\end{multlined}

(2.15)

\begin{multlined}\bigg(Z_{\bar{\chi}}^{\mathsf{c}}\,\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\eta(c)}X_{\bar{o}^{c}_{\mathsf{v}}(\chi)}^{\mathsf{v}}\bigg)\cdot{\mathcal{G}}\\
={\mathcal{G}}\cdot\bigg(\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\eta(c)}\,X_{\bar{o}^{c}_{\mathsf{v}}(\chi)}^{\mathsf{v}}\bigg).\end{multlined}

(2.16)

Given these identities, it is now straightforward to argue that the mutually commuting operators

\begin{gathered}\mathbb{a}^{\mathsf{v}}_{g}:=Z_{\bar{g}}^{\mathsf{v}}\otimes\bigg(\bigotimes_{c\in\eta^{-1}(\mathsf{v})}X^{\mathsf{c}}_{o^{c}_{\mathsf{v}}(g)}\bigg)\otimes Z_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}\\
\in{\rm End}\big(\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]^{\otimes|\mathsf{V}|}\otimes\mathbb{C}[G]^{\otimes|\mathsf{C}|}\otimes\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]^{\otimes|\mathsf{V}|}\big)\end{gathered}\,,

(2.17)

and

\begin{gathered}\mathbb{b}^{\mathsf{c}}_{\chi}:=Z^{\mathsf{c}}_{\bar{\chi}}\otimes\bigg(\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\eta(c)}X^{\mathsf{v}}_{\bar{o}^{c}_{\mathsf{v}}(\chi)}\bigg)\otimes Z^{\mathsf{c}}_{\chi}\\
\in{\rm End}\big(\mathbb{C}[G]^{\otimes|\mathsf{C}|}\otimes\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]^{\otimes|\mathsf{V}|}\otimes\mathbb{C}[G]^{\otimes|\mathsf{C}|}\big)\end{gathered}

(2.18)

are symmetries of the concatenated gauging maps
\widehat{\mathcal{G}}\circ\mathcal{G}
and
\mathcal{G}\circ\widehat{\mathcal{G}}
respectively. Indeed:

\displaystyle\mathbb{a}^{\mathsf{v}}_{g}\cdot\big(\widehat{\mathcal{G}}\circ\mathcal{G}\big)

\displaystyle=\widehat{\mathcal{G}}\circ\mathcal{G},

(2.19)

\displaystyle\mathbb{b}^{\mathsf{c}}_{\chi}\cdot\big(\mathcal{G}\circ\widehat{\mathcal{G}}\big)

\displaystyle=\mathcal{G}\circ\widehat{\mathcal{G}},

(2.20)

for all
\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)
,
\mathsf{c}\in\mathsf{C}(\Lambda)
,
g\in G
,
\chi\in\widehat{G}
. The iterated gauging procedure put forward in
[
12
]
now dictates that given any state
\ket{\psi}\in\mathcal{H}
stabilized by the initial
G
symmetry, that is

\mathbb{U}_{g}[\Omega]\ket{\psi}=\ket{\psi}

(2.21)

for every
valid
symmetry operator
\mathbb{U}_{g}[\Omega]
, one can define the
emergent
state
\ket{\Psi[\psi]}
as

\begin{gathered}\ket{\Psi[\psi]}:=\cdots\mathcal{G}_{\mathsf{\frac{3}{2}}}\circ\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathsf{1}}\circ\mathcal{G}_{\mathsf{\frac{1}{2}}}\ket{\psi}\\
\in\bigotimes_{\mathsf{\frac{i}{2}}}\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]^{\otimes|\mathsf{V}|}\bigotimes_{\mathsf{i}}\mathbb{C}[G]^{\otimes|\mathsf{C}|}\end{gathered}\,,

(2.22)

where the big tensor products run over all appearances of the gauging maps in the definition.

This state is then by construction stabilized by the operators
\mathbb{a}^{\mathsf{v}}_{g}
and
\mathbb{b}^{\mathsf{c}}_{\chi}
defined above. Given these stabilizers one can subsequently construct a stabilizer Hamiltonian for which
\ket{\Psi[\psi]}
is a ground state. Remark that additional stabilizers are given by the emergent symmetries of every gauging map. For the examples that follow we will refrain from including these stabilizers as they are in those cases non-local operators. However, note that this is by no means always the case. Recall that in the example of
, the emergent 1-form symmetries around individual plaquettes gave rise to the plaquette terms defined in
eq.

1.54
. In fact, we rather would like to think of these terms as kinematical constraints on the Hilbert space on which the emergent state is defined and as such we are allowed to include them in the Hamiltonian.

Given the foliated way in which the emergent state (
) is constructed it is now a sensible thing to consider this foliation as an additional dimension so that
\ket{\Psi[\psi]}
is a state that lives in exactly one dimension higher than the initial state
\ket{\psi}
. In this interpretation
\ket{\psi}
behaves as a boundary condition for the emergent state. The lattice on which
\ket{\Psi[\psi]}
is supported can then also be thought of as
emerging
from
\Lambda
on which
\ket{\psi}
is defined. More precisely, the lattice is made up of layers which each carry a copy of
\Lambda
. In every other layer
\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]
-valued degrees of freedom are placed on
\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)
and
\mathbb{C}[G]
-valued degrees of freedom supported on
\mathsf{C}(\Lambda)
. This is most easily demonstrated by concrete examples.

2.3
Gapped boundary conditions

In the interpretation of
\ket{\Psi[\psi]}
as a state living in one dimension higher than
\ket{\psi}
, the stabilizers
\mathbb{a}^{\mathsf{v}}_{g}
and
\mathbb{b}^{\mathsf{c}}_{\chi}
are interpreted as acting on the
bulk
of the state
\ket{\Psi[\psi]}
. The question of how to include boundary terms that stabilize
\ket{\Psi[\psi]}
poses itself. As it turns out, the answer to this question is intimately interwoven with the exact way in which the initial
G
symmetry is realized on the boundary state
\ket{\psi}
.

Let us begin by considering the simplest local candidate stabilizer. It can be verified readily that for a given
g\in G
and
\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)

\begin{gathered}Z_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}\otimes{\rm id}\\
\in{\rm End}\big(\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]^{\otimes|\mathsf{V}|}\otimes\mathbb{C}[G]^{\otimes|\mathsf{C}|}\big)\end{gathered}

(2.23)

commutes with the gauging map
\mathcal{G}
since it obviously commutes with the local gauge transformations
\mathcal{G}^{\mathsf{v}}_{g}
. Hence, it is a stabilizer of the emergent state exactly when it is one of the boundary condition, i.e.
Z_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}\ket{\psi}=\ket{\psi}
. Note that one could think of this operator as a ‘truncated’ vertex term
\mathbb{a}^{\mathsf{v}}_{g}
.

Consider likewise the truncated
\mathbb{b}^{\mathsf{c}}_{\chi}
term

\begin{gathered}{\rm id}\otimes Z_{\bar{\chi}}^{\mathsf{c}}\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\eta(c)}X^{\mathsf{v}}_{\bar{o}^{c}_{\mathsf{v}}(\chi)}\\
\in{\rm End}\big(\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]^{\otimes|\mathsf{V}|}\otimes\mathbb{C}[G]^{\otimes|\mathsf{C}|}\otimes\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]^{\otimes|\mathsf{V}|}\big)\end{gathered}\,,

(2.24)

Recall that the preimage of this operator under
\widehat{\mathcal{G}}\circ\mathcal{G}
was shown to be

\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\eta(c)}\,X_{\bar{o}^{c}_{\mathsf{v}}(\chi)}^{\mathsf{v}},

(2.25)

in
. This observation thus implies that the truncated term (
) is a stabilizer of the emergent state, whenever
\ket{\psi}
is stabilized by the check
X^{c}_{\bar{\chi}}
. Since these local constraints
X^{c}_{\chi}
can be understood as local symmetric order parameters for the global
G
symmetry (
), inequivalent boundary conditions realizing different symmetry breaking patterns of this symmetry can be devised. More formally, consider for any subgroup
H\leq G
the state
\ket{+}_{H}
which we recall was defined in
as
\ket{+}_{H}:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{|G/H|}}\sum_{[\chi]\in\widehat{G/H}}\ket{\chi}
. Constructing then the tensor product state

\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)}\ket{+}_{H}^{\mathsf{v}},

(2.26)

it is clear that this reference state is stabilized by
Z_{h}^{\mathsf{v}}
and
X^{c}_{\chi}
provided that
h\in H
, and
\chi\in\widehat{G/H}
. Remember indeed from
that
\widehat{G/H}
stands for the subgroup of characters in
\widehat{G}
which are trivial when restricted to
H
. From this it also follows that the corresponding boundary stabilizers of the emergent state
\ket{\Psi[\psi_H]}
commute. More generally, we could equally well consider boundary states of the form

\bigg(\sum_{[g]\in G/H}\mathbb{U}_{g}[\Omega]\bigg)\bigg(\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)}\ket{+}_{H}^{\mathsf{v}}\bigg)

(2.27)

for any allowed
\Omega
, which enjoy the same stabilizers.

Also remark that, depending on the specifics of the
G
symmetry generators, even more generic boundary conditions can be defined, for example by also (partially) breaking the translational invariance of the boundary state. An exhaustive study of gapped boundary conditions for the models under scrutiny will be the topic of future work.

3
Foliated type-I fracton order from 2D linear subsystem symmetries

In this section we showcase the gauging of abelian linear subsystem symmetries and their dual emergent symmetries, which are themselves linear subsystem symmetries on the dual lattice, following the prescription of
. Concatenation of these gauging maps results in foliated type-I fracton codes, generalizing the anisotropic models studied in
[
17
]
defined for cyclic groups to arbitrary finite abelian groups.

3.1
Gauging 2D abelian linear subsystem symmetries and their emergent symmetries

Throughout this section we consider again the two-dimensional torus, now endowed with a square lattice denoted by
\square
. The initial
\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]
-valued ‘matter’ degrees of freedom are located on the vertices
\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\square)
as customary. It will be useful to express the vertices in terms of their Cartesian coordinates as
\mathsf{v}\equiv(\mathsf{i},\mathsf{j})\in\mathbb{Z}_{L_{x}}\times\mathbb{Z}_{L_{y}}
. Naturally,
L_{x}
and
L_{y}
stand for the linear system size in the
x
and
y
direction respectively. The linear subsystem symmetry (LSS) generators are then represented on the matter Hilbert space
\mathcal{H}:=\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\square)}\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]
as

\displaystyle Z^{\hat{x},\mathsf{j}}_{g}:=\bigotimes_{\mathsf{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\!L_{x}}}Z_{g}^{(\mathsf{i},\,\mathsf{j})},

(3.1)

\displaystyle Z^{\hat{y},\mathsf{i}}_{g}:=\bigotimes_{\mathsf{j}\in\mathbb{Z}_{\!L_{y}}}Z_{g}^{(\mathsf{i},\,\mathsf{j})}.

(3.2)

There thus exists an extensive number of symmetry generators, one for every
\mathsf{j}
in the
\hat{x}
direction of the square lattice,
Z^{\hat{x},\mathsf{j}}_{g}
, and one for every
\mathsf{i}
in the
\hat{y}
direction,
Z^{\hat{y},\mathsf{i}}_{g}
. Notice however that not all of the symmetries generators are independent since clearly
\prod_{\mathsf{j}\in\mathbb{Z}_{L_{y}}}Z^{\hat{x},\mathsf{j}}_{g}=\prod_{\mathsf{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{L_{x}}}Z^{\hat{y},\mathsf{i}}_{g}
,
\forall g\in G
.

\color[rgb]{0.86,0.58,0.44}Z^{\hat{x},\mathsf{j}}_{g}
and
\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}Z^{\hat{y},\mathsf{i}}_{g^{\prime}}
on a portion of the square lattice looks like:

(3.3)

In order to employ the recipe of the general framework laid out in
we need to consider the checks that fully specify these symmetry generators. An adequate choice is given by

X^{c}_{\chi}=X_{\chi}^{(\mathsf{i},\,\mathsf{j})}\otimes X_{\bar{\chi}}^{(\mathsf{i}+1,\,\mathsf{j})}\otimes X_{\bar{\chi}}^{(\mathsf{i},\,\mathsf{j}+1)}\otimes X_{\chi}^{(\mathsf{i}+1,\,\mathsf{j}+1)},

(3.4)

\forall\chi\in\widehat{G}
,
\forall\mathsf{i},\mathsf{j}
. These operators are naturally associated with the plaquettes
\mathsf{P}(\square)
, and we will therefore identify the constraints with the plaquettes, i.e.
\mathcal{C}\ni c\equiv\mathsf{p}\in\mathsf{P}(\square)
. Indeed, graphically, one such operator can be depicted as

(3.5)

Let us continue by gauging this symmetry. To this end we introduce thus
\mathbb{C}[G]
-valued gauge fields on the plaquettes
\mathsf{p}\in\mathsf{P}(\square)
and thereby extend the Hilbert space according to
\mathcal{H}\rightarrow\mathcal{H}\otimes\widehat{\mathcal{H}}
, where
\widehat{\mathcal{H}}:=\bigotimes_{\mathsf{p}\in\mathsf{P}(\square)}\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]
. The local gauge transformations in the neighborhood of the vertex
\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\square)
read then

\mathcal{G}_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}:=Z_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}\,\bigotimes_{\mathsf{p}\rightarrow\mathsf{v}}\,X_{\bar{g}}^{\mathsf{p}}\,\bigotimes_{\mathsf{p}\leftarrow\mathsf{v}}\,X_{g}^{\mathsf{p}}\,,

(3.6)

for every
g\in G
. The tensor products appearing in this definition are over the sets of plaquettes
\mathsf{p}\rightarrow\mathsf{v}
, respectively
\mathsf{p}\leftarrow\mathsf{v}
, which point into, respectively point away from, the vertex
\mathsf{v}
according to the following orientations:

(3.7)

As such, the definition of
\mathcal{G}_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}
is in accordance with
. Notice that here the same
blue
and
red
color code of the previous sections for depicting degrees of freedom in respectively
\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]
and
\mathbb{C}[G]
is recycled.

As prescribed by our general gauging procedure, we define the following local projector:

\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{v}}:=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\mathcal{G}_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}\,,

(3.8)

for every vertex
\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\Lambda)
, out of which we construct the projector onto the gauge invariant subspace as:

\mathcal{P}:=\prod_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\square)}\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{v}}.

(3.9)

Gauging of the LSS then happens by initializing the gauge fields in the trivial tensor product configuration
\bigotimes_{\mathsf{p}\in\mathsf{P}(\square)}\ket{1}^{\mathsf{p}}
and applying the above projector
\mathcal{P}
so as to obtain

\mathcal{G}^{(0,1)}:=\mathcal{P}\bigg(\bigotimes_{\mathsf{p}\in\mathsf{P}(\square)}\ket{1}^{\mathsf{p}}\bigg).

(3.10)

The notation
\mathcal{G}^{(0,1)}
, following
[
19
]
, is motivated by the fact that there is a sense in which linear subsystem symmetries can be thought of as ‘
(0,1)
-form’ symmetries:
0
-form symmetries acting on a codimension
1
foliation of the spatial manifold. From the above definition of the gauging map it follows that it satisfies:

\displaystyle\mathcal{G}^{(0,1)}\cdot Z^{\hat{x},\mathsf{j}}_{g}

\displaystyle=\mathcal{G}^{(0,1)},

(3.11)

\displaystyle\mathcal{G}^{(0,1)}\cdot Z^{\hat{y},\mathsf{i}}_{g}

\displaystyle=\mathcal{G}^{(0,1)},

(3.12)

\forall g\in G
,
\mathsf{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{L_{x}}
,
\mathsf{j}\in\mathbb{Z}_{L_{y}}
. Hence, in line with the expectation from the general framework, states transforming non-trivially under one or more of the global linear subsystem symmetry generators are annihilated by the gauging map
\mathcal{G}^{(0,1)}
.

Let us now present the emergent symmetries. These happen to be themselves linear subsystem symmetries supported on the dual square lattice
\square^{\vee}
and are labeled by characters
\chi\in\widehat{G}
. Similarly as in the case of the initial LSS it proves useful to define the vertices of the dual square lattice,
\mathsf{v}^{\vee}\in\mathsf{V}(\square^{\vee})
, in terms of their Cartesian coordinates, i.e.
\mathsf{v}^{\vee}\equiv(\mathsf{i}^{\vee},\mathsf{j}^{\vee})\in\mathbb{Z}_{L_{y}}\times\mathbb{Z}_{L_{x}}
. Also notice that the dual vertices can be identified under Poincaré duality with the plaquettes of the primal square lattice, formally:
\mathsf{V}(\square^{\vee})\ni\mathsf{v}^{\vee}\equiv\mathsf{p}\in\mathsf{P}(\square)
. We then define for any character
\chi\in\widehat{G}
the
dual
LSS generators:

\displaystyle Z^{\hat{x}^{\vee}\!,\,\mathsf{j}^{\vee}}_{\chi}:=\bigotimes_{\mathsf{i}^{\vee}\in\mathbb{Z}_{L_{y}}}Z_{\chi}^{(\mathsf{i}^{\vee}\!,\,\mathsf{j}^{\vee})},

(3.13)

\displaystyle Z^{\hat{y}^{\vee}\!,\,\mathsf{i}^{\vee}}_{\chi}:=\bigotimes_{\mathsf{j}^{\vee}\in\mathbb{Z}_{L_{x}}}Z_{\chi}^{(\mathsf{i}^{\vee}\!,\,\mathsf{j}^{\vee})}.

(3.14)

Examples of
\color[rgb]{0.86,0.58,0.44}Z^{\hat{y}^{\vee}\!,\mathsf{j}^{\vee}}_{\chi}
and
\color[rgb]{0.5,0.5,0.5}Z^{\hat{x}^{\vee}\!,\mathsf{i}^{\vee}}_{\chi^{\prime}}
then look like

wherein the dual lattice
\square^{\vee}
is drawn in gray on top of the primal lattice

The emergent symmetries are apparent from

\displaystyle Z^{\hat{x}^{\vee}\!,\,\mathsf{j}^{\vee}}_{\chi}\cdot\mathcal{G}^{(0,1)}=\mathcal{G}^{(0,1)},

(3.15)

\displaystyle Z^{\hat{y}^{\vee}\!,\,\mathsf{i}^{\vee}}_{\chi}\cdot\mathcal{G}^{(0,1)}=\mathcal{G}^{(0,1)},

(3.16)

for all
\chi\in\widehat{G},\,\mathsf{i}^{\vee}\in\mathbb{Z}_{L_{y}},\,\mathsf{j}^{\vee}\in\mathbb{Z}_{L_{x}}
.

Despite these identities being a mere application of
to the case at hand, let us nevertheless derive these emergent symmetries explicitly for completeness. To this end, note that the operators
Z^{\hat{x}^{\vee}\!,\,\mathsf{j}^{\vee}}_{\chi},Z^{\hat{y}^{\vee}\!,\,\mathsf{i}^{\vee}}_{\chi}
commute with the projector in
and leave invariant the initial trivial gauge field on the plaquettes
\bigotimes_{\mathsf{p}\in\mathsf{P}(\square)}\ket{1}^{\mathsf{p}}
. The former is satisfied because along dual horizontal and vertical directions
\hat{x}^{\vee}/\hat{y}^{\vee}
, the operators
Z^{\hat{x}^{\vee}\!,\,\mathsf{j}^{\vee}}_{\chi},Z^{\hat{y}^{\vee}\!,\,\mathsf{i}^{\vee}}_{\chi}
overlap in two faces with the projectors
\mathcal{P}_{g}^{\mathsf{v}}
appearing in the definition of
\mathcal{G}^{(0,1)}
that act as
X_{g}\otimes X^{\dagger}_{g}
on them.

To conclude the construction of the
\mathcal{G}^{(0,1)}
gauging map, let us provide its PEPO representation. To this end we use tensors which slightly generalize those introduced in
. Their symmetry properties are therefore also completely analogous and are omitted here. Again restricting to one unit cell of the PEPO, which in this case is made up of one Z-type tensor on the vertex
\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\square)
of the unit cell and one
+
-type tensor on an adjacent plaquette
\mathsf{p}\in\mathsf{P}(\square)
, we claim that the PEPO is constructed from:

3.2
Iterative gauging of linear subsystem symmetries

Due to the structural similarity between the dual LSS generators (
3.13
,
3.14
) and the initial ones (
3.1
,
3.2
), the gauging procedure of the latter can be readily adopted to gauge the emergent LSS symmetries. To this end, we introduce
\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]
-valued gauge fields on the plaquettes
\mathsf{p}^{\vee}
of the dual lattice
\square^{\vee}
, which, as we mentioned, can equivalently be thought of as the vertices
\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\square)
. As is custom by now, we initiate these gauge fields as
\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\square)}\ket{\underline 1}^{\mathsf{v}}
. On this enlarged Hilbert space we define the local gauge transformation

\mathcal{G}_{\chi}^{\mathsf{p}}:=Z_{\chi}^{\mathsf{p}}\,\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\rightarrow\mathsf{p}}\,X_{\bar{\chi}}^{\mathsf{v}}\,\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\leftarrow\mathsf{p}}\,X_{\chi}^{\mathsf{v}}.

(3.18)

The orientations determining the sets of ‘incoming’ and ‘outgoing’ plaquettes on the dual square lattice, respectively
\mathsf{v}\rightarrow\mathsf{p}
and
\mathsf{v}\leftarrow\mathsf{p}
, are dual to those on the primal lattice as per the convention in (
). From the perspective of the primal lattice this gauge transformation can hence be depicted as

\scriptstyle X_{\!\chi}
\scriptstyle X_{\!\chi}^{\dagger}
\scriptstyle X_{\!\chi}^{\dagger}
\scriptstyle X_{\!\chi}
\scriptstyle Z_{\!\chi}
\mathcal{G}_{\chi}^{\mathsf{p}}

(3.19)

Using the local projectors

\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{p}}:=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{\chi\in\widehat{G}}\mathcal{G}_{\chi}^{\mathsf{p}}\,\,,

(3.20)

the following gauging map is then constructed:

\widehat{\mathcal{G}}^{(0,1)}:=\bigg(\prod_{\mathsf{p}\in\mathsf{P}(\square)}\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{p}}\bigg)\bigg(\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\square)}\ket{\underline 1}^{\mathsf{v}}\bigg).

(3.21)

After the application of
\widehat{\mathcal{G}}^{(0,1)}
LSSs on the primal lattice represented by (
3.1
-
3.2
) are reattained.

(3.22)

In this depiction it has to be understood that the dual Z-type tensor is placed on a plaquette
\mathsf{p}\in\mathsf{P}(\square)
of the lattice whereas the dual +-type tensor is located on a vertex
\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\square)
. The symmetries of this PEPO are immediately found from dualizing those of the above PEPO defined in
; from them the properties of
\widehat{\mathcal{G}}^{(0,1)}
are recovered immediately.

An initial state
\ket{\psi}
that is in the even sector of the LSSs (
3.1
-
3.2
) can now be iteratively gauged by using the usual prescription as follows:

\ket{\Psi[\psi]}:=\cdots\circ\mathcal{G}_{\mathsf{\frac{3}{2}}}^{(0,1)}\circ\widehat{\mathcal{G}}_{\mathsf{1}}^{(0,1)}\circ\mathcal{G}_{\mathsf{\frac{1}{2}}}^{(0,1)}\ket{\psi}.

(3.23)

Following our general paradigm we then interpret
\ket{\Psi[\psi]}
as a three-dimensional state living on a cubic lattice
endowed with a copy of
\mathbb{C}[\widehat{G}]
to every edge in the
\hat{z}
direction (
blue
) and a local Hilbert space
\mathbb{C}[G]
(
red
) associated to every plaquette in the
xy
-plane. Putting the PEPO representations
and
together, it then follows that the emergent state away from the boundary can be represented by the PEPO unit cell

(3.27)

in which

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{\mathsf{v}}

\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\mathbb{a}_{g}^{\mathsf{v}},

(3.28)

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{\mathsf{c}}

\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{\chi\in\widehat{G}}\mathbb{b}_{\chi}^{\mathsf{c}}.

(3.29)

This generalizes the anisotropic model introduced in
[

]
, which exhibits foliated type-I fracton order, to arbitrary finite groups. Our representation can be brought in the form showcased in
[
17
]
by applying the local basis transformation defined in
to the red plaquettes. It is expected that our approach will facilitate the classification and construction of these fracton orders.

for all
\chi\in\widehat{G}
and

.

Being truncated versions of the bulk stabilizers
\mathbb{b}^{\mathsf{c}}_{\chi}
and
\mathbb{a}^{\mathsf{v}}_{g}
, they naturally commute with all bulk terms appearing in the bulk Hamiltonian
\mathbb{H}^{\rm blk}
. Note that, similar as to the boundary terms defined for the introductory example in
,
\mathbb{d}^{\mathsf{c}}_{\chi}
and
\mathbb{c}^{\mathsf{e}_{z}}_{g}
only commute for particular choices of
\chi
and
g
such that
\chi(g)=1
. This statement will be refined below.

\mathbb{d}^{\mathsf{c}}_{\chi}
stabilizes the three-dimensional state
\ket{\Psi[\psi]}
if the boundary condition
\ket{\psi}
is symmetric under the operator
