4
Type-I fracton order from 2D Sierpinski fractal symmetry

In this section we consider
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
Sierpinski fractal symmetry as initial symmetry to our iterative gauging procedure. It is shown that the original Castelnovo-Chamon fractal model proposed in
[
18
]
emerges.

4.1
Gauging Sierpinski fractal symmetry and its emergent dual fractal symmetry

Let us begin by defining a set of generators for the fractal Sierpinski symmetry. Therefore we consider the two-dimensional torus endowed with a triangular lattice that we will denote by
\triangle
. Given a vertex
\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\triangle)
, we will denote its rectangular coordinates in the basis
\{\hat{x},\hat{y}\}
, indicated in the figure below, by
\mathsf{v}\equiv(\mathsf{i},\mathsf{j})
,
\mathsf{i},\mathsf{j}\in\mathbb{Z}_{L}
,
L
being the
linear system size
. Every vertex
\mathsf{v}
carries a copy of the local Hilbert space
\mathbb{C}[\mathbb{Z}_{2}]\simeq\mathbb{C}^{2}={\rm Span}_{\mathbb{C}}\{\ket{0},\ket{1}\}
on which the Pauli operators
X
and
Z
are defined.
7
7

7

In fact, in the remainder of this section we will identify
\mathbb{C}[\mathbb{Z}_{2}]
and
\mathbb{C}[\widehat{\mathbb{Z}_{2}}]
by making use of the obvious isomorphism
\mathbb{Z}_{2}\simeq\widehat{\mathbb{Z}}_{2}
.
We will consider a subset
\mathsf{P}(\triangle)^{+}\!\subset\!\mathsf{P}(\triangle)
of the plaquettes whose member plaquettes are shaded in red in the figure below, foreshadowing that we will put gauge degrees of freedom on these plaquettes when gauging the fractal symmetry. Note that the number of such plaquettes equals the number of vertices, i.e.
|\mathsf{P}(\triangle)^{+}|=|\mathsf{V}(\triangle)|
.
8
8

8

Indeed, this follows from the fact that the Euler characteristic of the torus is zero, which can be expressed as
|\mathsf{V}(\triangle)|-|\mathsf{E}(\triangle)|+|\mathsf{P}(\triangle)|=0
, combined with the facts that
|\mathsf{P}(\triangle)|=2|\mathsf{P}(\triangle)^{+}|
and
|\mathsf{E}(\triangle)|=3|\mathsf{V}(\triangle)|
.
This allows us to assign to every
\mathsf{p}^{+}\in\mathsf{P}(\triangle)^{+}
a
base point

{\rm bp}(\mathsf{p}^{+})
which we conventionally choose as dictated by the dotted lines in the figure:

(4.1)

As pointed out in
[
36
]
the number of symmetry generators depends in a non-trivial way on the (linear) system size
L
. In this section we will for demonstrative purposes restrict to the case of
L=2^{m}-1
for an integer
m
, in which case the number of symmetry generators is exactly equal to
L-1
. The Sierpinski symmetry generators are then of the form

\mathbb{U}[\mathcal{S}_{q}]:=\prod_{\mathsf{i},\mathsf{j}}\big(Z^{(\mathsf{i},\mathsf{j})}\big)^{\mathcal{S}_{q}(\mathsf{i},\mathsf{j})},

(4.2)

where
\mathcal{S}_{q}
is a function
\mathcal{S}_{q}:\mathbb{Z}_{L}\times\mathbb{Z}_{L}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{2}
defined such that
\mathbb{U}[\mathcal{S}_{q}]
commutes with the checks
X^{\mathsf{p}^{+}}
which are given by

\begin{gathered}X^{\mathsf{p}^{+}}:=X^{(\mathsf{i},\mathsf{j})}\otimes X^{(\mathsf{i}+1,\mathsf{j})}\otimes X^{(\mathsf{i},\mathsf{j}+1)},\\
(\mathsf{i},\mathsf{j})={\rm bp}(\mathsf{p}^{+}),\end{gathered}

(4.3)

for all
\mathsf{p}^{+}\in\mathsf{P}(\triangle)^{+}
. A check thus consists of three Pauli
X
operators acting on the three vertices surrounding a plaquette
\mathsf{p}^{+}\in\mathsf{P}(\triangle)^{+}
.

As follows from a direct computation, imposing commutation of the generators (
) with all these checks requires
\mathcal{S}_{q}
to satisfy the recursive identity

\mathcal{S}_{q}(\mathsf{i},\mathsf{j}+1):=\mathcal{S}_{q}(\mathsf{i}+1,\mathsf{j})+\mathcal{S}_{q}(\mathsf{i},\mathsf{j}),

(4.4)

\forall\ \mathsf{i},\mathsf{j}\in\mathbb{Z}_{L}
. A
valid symmetry generator
is hence fully specified by a
valid
choice of ‘initial condition’ at
\mathsf{j}=0
:

\mathcal{S}_{q}(\mathsf{i},0):=q(\mathsf{i})\in\mathbb{F}_{2}^{L}.

(4.5)

The function
\mathcal{S}_{q}(\mathsf{i},\mathsf{j})
, for
\mathsf{j}\neq 0
follows then from applying the recursion relation to this choice of
q
, and as such the corresponding generator
\mathbb{U}[\mathcal{S}_{q}]
commutes by construction with all checks. The
L-1
independent choices for
q
which give rise to the
L-1
independent Sierpinski symmetry generators that we expect can be chosen as

q^{(\alpha)}(\mathsf{i})=\delta_{\mathsf{i},\alpha}+\delta_{\mathsf{i},\alpha+1},\quad\alpha=1,2,...,L-1.

(4.6)

Let us mention as a side remark that it turns out that one could think of
\mathcal{S}_{q}
as a
valid history
of a
Sierpinski cellular automaton
in the following sense. For fixed
\mathsf{j}
,
\mathcal{S}(\mathsf{i},\mathsf{j})
corresponds to a state valued in
\mathbb{F}_{2}^{L}
. Given this state, the state at
\mathsf{j}+1
, i.e.
\mathcal{S}_{q}(\mathsf{i},\mathsf{j}+1)
for fixed
\mathsf{j}+1
, is fully specified by the above recursion relation from
\mathcal{S}_{q}(\mathsf{i},\mathsf{j})
. Therefore
\mathsf{j}
can be thought of as labeling discrete ‘time’ steps, where this notion of time thus flows in the direction of increasing
\mathsf{j}
. In this picture
q(\mathsf{i})
serves as an initial condition for the automaton, a posteriori justifying our jargon introduced above.

As a concrete example take
L=3
, and
q^{(1)}(\mathsf{i})=[1\ 1\ 0]_{\mathsf{i}}
. The corresponding history
\mathcal{S}_{q}
is then computed to be

\mathcal{S}_{q}(\mathsf{i},\mathsf{j})=\begin{bmatrix}1&1&0\\
0&1&1\\
1&0&1\end{bmatrix}_{\mathsf{j},\mathsf{i}},

(4.7)

whose matching lattice operator
\mathbb{U}[\mathcal{S}_{q}]
can be depicted as:

(4.8)

Let us now gauge the Sierpinski symmetry using the general paradigm of
. To this end we introduce qubit gauge degrees of freedom on the plaquettes in
\mathsf{P}(\triangle)^{+}
. A local gauge transformation for every
\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\triangle)
reads then

\mathcal{G}^{\mathsf{v}}_{1}:=Z^{\mathsf{v}}\!\!\!\!\bigotimes_{\mathsf{p}^{+}\in\mathsf{P}(\triangle)^{+}|\mathsf{v}}X^{\mathsf{p}^{+}},

(4.9)

wherein the tensor product is understood to be over plaquettes
\mathsf{p}^{+}\in\mathsf{P}(\triangle)^{+}|\mathsf{v}
that contain
\mathsf{v}
. Graphically:

(4.10)

From the local projector

\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{v}}:=\frac{1}{2}\left({\rm id}+\mathcal{G}^{\mathsf{v}}_{1}\right),

(4.11)

one constructs, as is by now routine, the global projector
\mathcal{P}=\prod_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\triangle)}\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{v}}
from which one obtains the gauging map by trivially initializing the gauge field:

\mathcal{G}:=\mathcal{P}\bigg(\bigotimes_{\mathsf{p}\in\mathsf{P}(\triangle)^{+}}\ket{0}^{\mathsf{p}}\bigg).

(4.12)

Evidently, one has
\mathcal{G}^{\mathsf{v}}_{1}\cdot\mathcal{G}=\mathcal{G}
. Let us also verify explicitly that this gauging map indeed projects out states transforming non-trivially under the Sierpinski symmetry, i.e.
\mathcal{G}\cdot\mathbb{U}[\mathcal{S}_{q}]=\mathcal{G}
, for all
valid
symmetry generators defined in
. To this end, we could expand the local projectors appearing in the definition of the gauging map
\mathcal{G}
:

\prod_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\triangle)}\prod_{\{g_{\mathsf{v}}\}_{\mathsf{v}}}(\mathcal{G}_{1}^{\mathsf{v}})^{g_{\mathsf{v}}}.

(4.13)

From the definition of
\mathcal{G}_{1}^{\mathsf{v}}
in
it then follows that three
\mathcal{G}_{1}^{\mathsf{v}}
’s in the expansion (
) on vertices
(\mathsf{i}+1,\mathsf{j})
,
(\mathsf{i},\mathsf{j})
and
(\mathsf{i},\mathsf{j}+1)
overlap in exactly one plaquette
\mathsf{p}^{+}\in\mathsf{P}(\triangle)^{+}
, namely the one such that
(\mathsf{i},\mathsf{j})={\rm bp}(\mathsf{p}^{+})
. Locally, this means that the property
\mathcal{G}\cdot\mathbb{U}[\mathcal{S}_{q}]=\mathcal{G}
is equivalent to
\mathcal{S}_{q}
satisfying (
), which it has to in order to define a genuine Sierpinski symmetry generator.

We now turn to the emergent symmetries. As a matter of fact, after gauging we obtain a
dual
Sierpinski fractal symmetry supported on the gauge degrees of freedom. Given a plaquette
\mathsf{p}^{+}\in\mathsf{P}(\triangle)^{+}
, we define its
rectangular coordinates
as
(\mathsf{i}^{\vee},\mathsf{j}^{\vee}):={\rm bp}(\mathsf{p}^{+})
. Mimicking the definition of
\mathcal{S}_{q}
, let us define
\mathcal{S}_{q}^{\vee}:\mathbb{Z}_{L}\times\mathbb{Z}_{L}\rightarrow\mathbb{F}_{2}
by means of the recursive identity

\begin{multlined}\mathcal{S}_{q}^{\vee}(\mathsf{i}^{\vee},\mathsf{j}^{\vee}):=\mathcal{S}_{q}^{\vee}(\mathsf{i}^{\vee},\mathsf{j}^{\vee}+1)\\
+\mathcal{S}_{q}^{\vee}(\mathsf{i}^{\vee}-1,j^{\vee}+1)\end{multlined}\,,

(4.14)

\mathcal{S}_{q}^{\vee}(\mathsf{i}^{\vee},0):=q(\mathsf{i}^{\vee}),

(4.15)

for all
\mathsf{i}^{\vee},\mathsf{j}^{\vee}\in\mathbb{Z}_{L}
. By comparison with the definition of
\mathcal{S}_{q}
in (
) we can infer that
\mathcal{S}_{q}^{\vee}
defines a Sierpinski fractal symmetry in which the ‘time steps’ labeled by
\mathsf{j}
flow in the opposite direction compared to the one in (
) and in which the ‘spatial direction’
\mathsf{i}
is reflected as well.
It can then be shown that
\mathcal{S}_{q}^{\vee}
exactly specifies the emergent fractal symmetries after gauging. Namely, defining

\mathbb{U}^{\vee}[\mathcal{S}_{q}^{\vee}]:=\prod_{\mathsf{i}^{\vee},\mathsf{j}^{\vee}}(Z^{(\mathsf{i}^{\vee},\mathsf{j}^{\vee})})^{\mathcal{S}^{\vee}_{q}(\mathsf{i}^{\vee},\mathsf{j}^{\vee})},

(4.16)

it follows that

\mathbb{U}^{\vee}[\mathcal{S}_{q}^{\vee}]\cdot\mathcal{G}=\mathcal{G}.

(4.17)

Indeed, this follows from the fact that exactly for this choice of
\mathcal{S}^{\vee}_{q}
the operator
\mathbb{U}^{\vee}[\mathcal{S}_{q}^{\vee}]
commutes with every
\mathcal{G}_{1}^{\mathsf{v}}
,
\mathbb{U}^{\vee}[\mathcal{S}_{q}^{\vee}]\cdot\mathcal{G}_{1}^{\mathsf{v}}=\mathcal{G}_{1}^{\mathsf{v}}\cdot\mathbb{U}^{\vee}[\mathcal{S}_{q}^{\vee}]
, together with the trivial observation that the initial flat gauge configuration
\bigotimes_{\mathsf{p}^{+}\in\mathsf{P}(\triangle)^{+}}\ket{0}^{\mathsf{p}^{+}}
is a
+1
eigenstate of
\mathbb{U}^{\vee}[\mathcal{S}_{q}^{\vee}]
.

Since we are dealing with the symmetry group
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
here, we can in fact significantly simplify the tensor network calculus introduced in
by removing the arrows and using a
red
color for all tensor legs since we have identified
\mathbb{C}[\mathbb{Z}_{2}]
and
\mathbb{C}[\widehat{\mathbb{Z}_{2}}]
above. By virtue of these simplifications, we will also only need two type of tensors for both gauging maps which are given by:

{\rm bp}(\mathsf{p}^{+})

4.2
Iterative gauging of Sierpinski fractal symmetry

Gauging of the dual Sierpinski symmetry happens via the introduction of qubits on the vertices
\mathsf{V}(\triangle)
.
In the neighborhood of a plaquette
\mathsf{p}^{+}\in\mathsf{P}(\triangle)^{+}
, following gauge transformation is defined:

\mathcal{G}_{1}^{\mathsf{p}^{+}}:=Z^{\mathsf{p}^{+}}\!\!\!\!\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\triangle)|\mathsf{p}^{+}}X^{\mathsf{v}},

(4.21)

which forms a local
\mathbb{Z}_{2}
-representation. In this,
\mathsf{V}(\triangle)|\mathsf{p}^{+}
stands for the set of three vertices surrounding
\mathsf{p}^{+}
. Concretely:

(4.22)

Based on the local projector, defined as

\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{p}^{+}}:=\frac{1}{2}\left({\rm id}+\mathcal{G}_{1}^{\mathsf{p}^{+}}\right),

(4.23)

the corresponding gauging map reads:

\widehat{\mathcal{G}}:=\mathcal{P}\bigg(\bigotimes_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}(\triangle)}\ket{0}^{\mathsf{v}}\bigg),

(4.24)

in which
\mathcal{P}:=\prod_{\mathsf{p}^{+}\in\mathsf{P}(\triangle)^{+}}\mathcal{P}^{\mathsf{p}^{+}}
. The expected properties
\mathbb{U}[\mathcal{S}_{q}]\cdot\widehat{\mathcal{G}}=\widehat{\mathcal{G}}
and
\widehat{\mathcal{G}}\cdot\mathbb{U}^{\vee}[\mathcal{S}^{\vee}_{q}]=\widehat{\mathcal{G}}
, for all valid symmetry generators
\mathbb{U}[\mathcal{S}_{q}]
and
\mathbb{U}^{\vee}[\mathcal{S}_{q}^{\vee}]
, hold by construction.

Under the aforementioned conventions, the unit cell of the PEPO representation of
\widehat{\mathcal{G}}
can be depicted as

(4.25)

where now the Z-type tensor is placed on a plaquette
\mathsf{p}^{+}\in\mathsf{P}(\triangle)^{+}
and the second tensor on the corresponding base point.

What is the emergent state obtained from these gauging procedures? It turns out that the emergent state can be interpreted as living on the vertices of a
hexagonal close-packed
(HCP) lattice, which consists of layers of triangular lattices whose vertices are slightly displaced with respect to each other
[
37
]
. A slightly different realization of this lattice which is closer to our setup is the following. We consider also layers of two-dimensional triangular lattices
\triangle
, but in such a way that the vertices of all layers align along the direction perpendicular to the stack of layers. In every other layer we then place qubits on the vertices of the triangular lattice, i.e. on
\mathsf{V}(\triangle)
, and on the plaquettes
\mathsf{P}(\triangle)^{+}
.
The PEPO representation of the emergent state for one unit cell is then given by:

(4.28)

With slight abuse of notation,
\mathsf{v}
refers to the vertex of the emergent lattice on which the bottom
blue
qubit appearing in the
\mathbb{a}
operator is supported. On the other hand,
\mathsf{p}^{+}
refers to the support of the
red
qubit on the bottom of the depiction of the
\mathbb{b}^{\mathsf{p}^{+}}
operator. It is clear that these operators all mutually commute. We can construct projectors out of these operators as

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{\mathsf{v}}:=\frac{1}{2}\big({\rm id}+\mathbb{a}^{\mathsf{v}}\big),

(4.29)

\displaystyle\mathbb{P}^{\mathsf{p}^{+}}:=\frac{1}{2}\big({\rm id}+\mathbb{b}^{\mathsf{p}^{+}}\big).

(4.30)

The emergent bulk Hamiltonian then reads

\mathbb{H}^{\rm blk}:=-\sum_{\mathsf{v}\in\mathsf{V}}\mathbb{P}^{\mathsf{v}}-\sum_{\mathsf{p}^{+}\in\mathsf{P}^{+}}\mathbb{P}^{\mathsf{p}^{+}},

(4.31)

where the sums are over all (bulk) vertices and
\mathsf{p}^{+}
-plaquettes of the HCP lattice. This model was proposed by Caselnovo and Chamon in
[
18
]
, is covered in the family of models by Yoshida
[
38
]
and was recently studied in detail in
[
37
]
.

If we start the iterative gauging by
\mathcal{G}
, the possible boundary terms correspond to the truncation of (
4.27
) near the boundary or individual
Z
terms.
Explicitly the truncated (
4.27
) terms read:

(4.33)

which can be recognized as the local checks
X^{\mathsf{p}^{+}}
and serve as a local order parameter for the initial fractal symmetry. As such, there are two possible boundaries depending on whether the fractal symmetry is spontaneously broken by
\ket{\psi}
or not. In the first case, the boundary stabilizers are given by

\mathbb{Q}^{\mathsf{p}^{+}}:=\frac{1}{2}\bigg({\rm id}+X^{\mathsf{p}^{+}}\bigg),

(4.34)

for all
\mathsf{p}^{+}\in\mathsf{P}(\triangle)^{+}
on the boundary
\triangle
, whereas in the symmetry breaking case the stabilizers are given by

\mathbb{Q}^{\mathsf{p}^{+}}:=\frac{1}{2}\bigg({\rm id}+Z^{\mathsf{v}}\bigg).

(4.35)

5
Conclusion and outlook

In this work we have put the iterative gauging paradigm of
[
12
]
for abelian symmetries on a systematic footing and extended it to arbitrary dimensions and generic types of abelian symmetries. We provided explicit examples where the emergent states are three-dimensional. Concretely we have shown the emergence of surface codes, foliated type-I fracton codes and non-foliated type-I fracton codes from the iterative gauging of 0-form, 1-form, linear subsystem and Sierpinski fractal symmetry respectively.

The method proposed in this work resembles the
sandwich
construction of SymTFT. In particular, we constructed states of the following form:

\langle\hat{\psi}|\mathcal{G}\circ\widehat{\mathcal{G}}\circ\cdots\circ\mathcal{G}\circ\widehat{\mathcal{G}}\circ\mathcal{G}\ket{\psi},

made up of the gauging operator
\mathcal{G}
of a
G
symmetry, its dual
\widehat{\mathcal{G}}
and states
\ket{\psi},|\hat{\psi}\rangle
symmetric under the initial abelian symmetry and its dual. For the case where the boundary supports an abelian 1-form symmetry, our method exactly recovers the quantum double in correspondence with the SymTFT proposal. The symmetries of this sandwich state are considered as stabilizer local Hamiltonian terms giving rise to the Hamiltonian:

\mathbb{H}^{\rm blk}+\mathbb{H}^{\rm bdry},

where the bulk terms only depend on the symmetry
G
and the boundary terms depend on the quantum phase of
\ket{\psi}
.

We predict a number of ways in which this framework can be further refined and propose the following open problems. From the case of the emergent surface codes, it is clear that further refinement is required to accommodate boundary conditions hosting SPT phases on top of the partial symmetry breaking. It is plausible that akin to the lower-dimensional case
[
12
]
this requires modification of the boundary stabilizers. A similar question arises regarding the boundary conditions of the emergent anisotropic models studied in
. In particular, it would be revealing to study boundaries that (potentially partially) break translation symmetry. It is plausible to expect that by including boundary states which realize different symmetry breaking patterns in distinct regions, we could realize domain walls in the emergent orders such as the electromagnetic domain wall in the three-dimensional toric code
[
22
]
. One could also wonder to what extent our framework is exhaustive in producing classes stabilizer codes.

The main assumption of this work is the symmetry group being abelian, which results in abelian higher-dimensional codes. As such we leave the study of non-abelian, and more general categorical, symmetries in the iterative gauging framework for future work. As a first step, we will generalize the one-dimensional gauging map of
[
13
]
to generalized symmetries described by unitary fusion categories in forthcoming work
[
39
]
.

An obvious family of models not treated in this work are type-II fracton models, which differ from type-I fracton models in the mobility of their excitations. Adapting our approach to accommodate these fracton orders could prove to be a splendid challenge.

We further foresee that the explicit tensor network constructions of the states provided here will enhance their numerical study. Having direct access to the boundary states in this framework could facilitate the study of boundary phase transitions of these emergent models.
